@@@ topology-MnR-convergence-entries.md
---
title: Convergence in $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ via entries
category: topology/topology-of-mnr
level: l1
difficulty: 2
tags: matrix convergence, entrywise convergence, sequence of matrices
date: 2026-11-04
---

## Statement

A sequence $(A^{(k)})_{k\ge1}$ of matrices in $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ is said to *converge entrywise* to $A\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ if for every $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the real sequence $(a^{(k)}_{ij})_{k\ge1}$ converges to $a_{ij}$. Show that entrywise convergence is equivalent to convergence for the metric
$$d(A,B)=\max_{i,j}|a_{ij}-b_{ij}|.$$

## Hint

Compare $d(A^{(k)},A)$ with the largest entrywise difference; use the fact that a maximum of finitely many quantities vanishes iff each one vanishes.

## Solution

**$(\Leftarrow)$.** Suppose $d(A^{(k)},A)\to0$. For each $(i,j)$, $|a^{(k)}_{ij}-a_{ij}|\le d(A^{(k)},A)\to0$, so entrywise convergence holds.

**$(\Rightarrow)$.** Suppose entrywise convergence. For each $(i,j)$, $|a^{(k)}_{ij}-a_{ij}|\to0$. There are finitely many pairs $(i,j)$, so
$$d(A^{(k)},A)=\max_{i,j}|a^{(k)}_{ij}-a_{ij}|\to0.$$

**Conclusion.** Entrywise convergence and convergence for the sup metric coincide on $M_n(\mathbb{R})$.

@@@ topology-MnR-metrics-equivalent.md
---
title: Equivalent metrics on $M_n(\mathbb{R})$
category: topology/topology-of-mnr
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: equivalent metrics, norms on matrices, finite dimension
date: 2026-11-04
---

## Statement

Consider the following three norms on $M_n(\mathbb{R})$:
$$\|A\|_\infty=\max_{i,j}|a_{ij}|,\qquad \|A\|_1=\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|,\qquad \|A\|_F=\left(\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^2\right)^{1/2}.$$
Show that they are equivalent.

## Hint

Bound each by the others using the number of entries $n^2$.

## Solution

**Bounds.** For every $A\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$:
$$\|A\|_\infty\le\|A\|_F\le\|A\|_1\le n^2\|A\|_\infty.$$
- $\|A\|_\infty\le\|A\|_F$: each entry squared is $\le\sum|a_{ij}|^2$.
- $\|A\|_F\le\|A\|_1$: from $\|A\|_F^2=\sum|a_{ij}|^2\le(\sum|a_{ij}|)^2$.
- $\|A\|_1\le n^2\|A\|_\infty$: sum of $n^2$ terms each $\le\|A\|_\infty$.

**Conclusion.** The three norms define the same topology on $M_n(\mathbb{R})$.

@@@ topology-MnR-complete.md
---
title: Completeness of $M_n(\mathbb{R})$
category: topology/topology-of-mnr
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: completeness, Cauchy sequence, identification with R^{n^2}
date: 2026-11-04
---

## Statement

Show that $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ equipped with the sup metric is complete.

## Hint

Identify $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ with $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$; use completeness of $\mathbb{R}$.

## Solution

**Identification.** The map $\Phi:M_n(\mathbb{R})\to\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ sending $A$ to its entries is an isometry for the sup metric.

**Cauchy sequences.** A Cauchy sequence in $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ corresponds to a Cauchy sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$. Since $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ is complete, it converges; identifying back gives convergence in $M_n(\mathbb{R})$.

**Conclusion.** $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ is complete.

@@@ topology-MnR-closed-subgroups.md
---
title: Classical closed subgroups of $GL_n(\mathbb{R})$
category: topology/topology-of-mnr
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: closed subgroups, GL_n, SL_n, O_n, determinant
date: 2026-11-04
---

## Statement

Show that the following subsets of $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ are closed:
$$SL_n(\mathbb{R})=\{A:\det A=1\},\qquad O_n(\mathbb{R})=\{A:A^TA=I_n\},\qquad S_n(\mathbb{R})=\{A:A^T=A\}.$$

## Hint

Each is the preimage of a closed set under a continuous map.

## Solution

**$SL_n$.** The determinant $\det:M_n(\mathbb{R})\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous (polynomial in the entries). $SL_n=\det^{-1}(\{1\})$ is closed as preimage of the closed set $\{1\}$.

**$O_n$.** The map $\Phi(A)=A^TA-I_n$ is continuous into the symmetric matrices. $O_n=\Phi^{-1}(\{0\})$ is closed.

**$S_n$.** The map $A\mapsto A^T-A$ is linear (continuous). $S_n$ is its kernel, hence closed.

**Conclusion.** $SL_n$, $O_n$, $S_n$ are closed subgroups (or subspace) of $M_n(\mathbb{R})$.

@@@ topology-MnR-open-GLn.md
---
title: $GL_n(\mathbb{R})$ is open in $M_n(\mathbb{R})$
category: topology/topology-of-mnr
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: GL_n, open set, determinant continuity
date: 2026-11-04
---

## Statement

Show that $GL_n(\mathbb{R})=\{A:\det A\neq0\}$ is open in $M_n(\mathbb{R})$.

## Hint

$\det$ is continuous and $GL_n=\det^{-1}(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\})$.

## Solution

**Argument.** $\det:M_n(\mathbb{R})\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous, and $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ is open. Therefore $GL_n=\det^{-1}(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\})$ is open.

**Conclusion.** $GL_n(\mathbb{R})$ is open, and its complement $SL_n$ (as well as $\{\det=0\}$) is closed.

@@@ topology-MnR-compact-groups.md
---
title: Compactness of orthogonal and orthogonal groups
category: topology/topology-of-mnr
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: compactness, O_n, SO_n, boundedness
date: 2026-11-04
---

## Statement

Show that $O_n(\mathbb{R})$ and $SO_n(\mathbb{R})=\{A\in O_n:\det A=1\}$ are compact subsets of $M_n(\mathbb{R})$.

## Hint

$O_n$ is closed (previous exercise) and bounded: every entry of an orthogonal matrix satisfies $|a_{ij}|\le1$.

## Solution

**Closed.** $O_n=\Phi^{-1}(\{0\})$ with $\Phi(A)=A^TA-I_n$, continuous: closed.

**Bounded.** For $A\in O_n$ and any row $i$: $\|(\text{row }i)\|_2=1$, so $|a_{ij}|\le1$. Hence $\|A\|_\infty\le1$: bounded.

**Conclusion.** $O_n$ is closed and bounded, hence compact (Heine–Borel in $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$). $SO_n$ is closed (as $O_n\cap SL_n$) and bounded, hence compact.

@@@ topology-MnR-compact-trace-zero.md
---
title: A non-compact closed subspace: trace-zero matrices
category: topology/topology-of-mnr
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: closed unbounded, trace, non-compactness
date: 2026-11-04
---

## Statement

Let $H=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb{R}):\operatorname{tr}(A)=0\}$. Show that $H$ is closed but not compact.

## Hint

$H$ is the kernel of the trace functional; show it is unbounded.

## Solution

**Closed.** The trace is linear, hence continuous; $H=\operatorname{tr}^{-1}(\{0\})$ is closed.

**Not compact.** The matrices $A_k=k\,E_{12}$ have trace $0$ for every $k$, but $\|A_k\|_\infty=k\to+\infty$: unbounded.

**Conclusion.** $H$ is closed and unbounded, hence not compact.

@@@ topology-MnR-interior.md
---
title: Interior and boundary of $GL_n(\mathbb{R})$
category: topology/topology-of-mnr
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: interior, boundary, GL_n
date: 2026-11-04
---

## Statement

Determine the interior and the boundary of $GL_n(\mathbb{R})$ in $M_n(\mathbb{R})$.

## Hint

$GL_n$ is open; its boundary is the set of singular matrices.

## Solution

**Interior.** Since $GL_n$ is open, $\mathring{GL_n}=GL_n$.

**Closure.** Every singular matrix $A$ is a limit of invertible matrices: $A+\varepsilon I$ is invertible for small $\varepsilon>0$. So $\overline{GL_n}=M_n(\mathbb{R})$.

**Boundary.** $\partial GL_n=\overline{GL_n}\setminus\mathring{GL_n}=M_n(\mathbb{R})\setminus GL_n$, the set of singular matrices.

**Conclusion.** Interior $=GL_n$; boundary $=$ singular matrices.

@@@ topology-MnR-distance-to-groups.md
---
title: Distance to $O_n$ and polar decomposition (statement)
category: topology/topology-of-mnr
level: m1
difficulty: 5
tags: distance to O_n, singular values, polar decomposition
date: 2026-11-04
---

## Statement

Show that for any $A\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$, the distance to $O_n$ for $\|\cdot\|_2$ is
$$\operatorname{dist}_2(A,O_n)=\max_i\bigl|\sigma_i(A)-1\bigr|,$$
where $\sigma_i(A)$ are the singular values of $A$.

## Hint

Use the polar decomposition $A=U\Sigma V^T$ with $U,V\in O_n$, $\Sigma$ diagonal nonnegative.

## Solution

**Polar decomposition.** Every real $A$ is $U\Sigma V^T$ with $U,V$ orthogonal and $\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n)\ge0$.

**Lower bound.** For any $Q\in O_n$, $\|A-Q\|_2=\|\Sigma-V^TQU\|_2=\|\Sigma-R\|_2$ where $R=V^TQU\in O_n$. Since $R$ is orthogonal, its singular values are all $1$, so $\|\Sigma-R\|_2\ge\max_i|\sigma_i-1|$.

**Upper bound.** Setting $Q=UV^T\in O_n$, one has $\|A-Q\|_2=\|\Sigma-I\|_2=\max_i|\sigma_i-1|$.

**Conclusion.** $\operatorname{dist}_2(A,O_n)=\max_i|\sigma_i(A)-1|$.

@@@ topology-MnR-matrix-exponential.md
---
title: Continuity of the matrix exponential
category: topology/topology-of-mnr
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: matrix exponential, continuity, series
date: 2026-11-04
---

## Statement

Show that $\exp:M_n(\mathbb{R})\to M_n(\mathbb{R})$, $\exp(A)=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{A^k}{k!}$, is continuous.

## Hint

Bound $\|\exp(A)-\exp(B)\|$ using the series and the inequality $\|A^k-B^k\|\le\|A-B\|\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\|A\|^j\|B\|^{k-1-j}$. Or use local boundedness and uniform convergence on bounded sets.

## Solution

**Local bound.** Fix $R>0$ and $A,B$ with $\|A\|,\|B\|\le R$. For each $k\ge1$:
$$\|A^k-B^k\|\le\|A-B\|\cdot kR^{k-1}.$$
Summing: $\|\exp(A)-\exp(B)\|\le\|A-B\|\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{kR^{k-1}}{k!}=\|A-B\|\,e^R$.

**Conclusion.** $\exp$ is locally Lipschitz on $M_n(\mathbb{R})$, hence continuous.

@@@ topology-MnR-eigenvalue-continuity.md
---
title: Continuity of eigenvalues (statement)
category: topology/topology-of-mnr
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: eigenvalues, continuity, roots of polynomial
date: 2026-11-04
---

## Statement

Show that the multiset of eigenvalues of a matrix depends continuously on the matrix entries.

## Hint

Eigenvalues are roots of the characteristic polynomial $\chi_A(\lambda)=\det(\lambda I-A)$, whose coefficients depend continuously on $A$; the roots of a monic polynomial depend continuously on its coefficients.

## Solution

**Characteristic polynomial.** $A\mapsto\chi_A$ is continuous (composition of $\det$ and affine maps).

**Root continuity.** A monic polynomial's roots (with multiplicity) depend continuously on the coefficients in the Hausdorff metric on finite multisets of $\mathbb{C}$.

**Conclusion.** Eigenvalues depend continuously on the matrix.

@@@ topology-MnR-separability.md
---
title: Separability of $M_n(\mathbb{R})$
category: topology/topology-of-mnr
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: separability, dense countable subset, rational matrices
date: 2026-11-04
---

## Statement

Show that $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ is separable.

## Hint

Consider matrices with rational entries.

## Solution

**Countable dense subset.** Let $M_n(\mathbb{Q})$ be the set of matrices with rational entries. It is countable (finite product of countable sets).

**Density.** For any $A\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ and $\varepsilon>0$, approximate each entry $a_{ij}$ by a rational $q_{ij}$ with $|a_{ij}-q_{ij}|<\varepsilon$. The matrix $Q=(q_{ij})$ satisfies $\|A-Q\|_\infty<\varepsilon$.

**Conclusion.** $M_n(\mathbb{Q})$ is countable and dense in $M_n(\mathbb{R})$, which is separable.

@@@ topology-MnR-norm-submultiplicative.md
---
title: Submultiplicativity of matrix norms
category: topology/topology-of-mnr
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: submultiplicative norms, operator norm, matrix norm
date: 2026-11-04
---

## Statement

Define $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{\|x\|=1}\|Ax\|$ (for $\|\cdot\|$ the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$). Show that $\|AB\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}$.

## Hint

Write $\|ABx\|\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|Bx\|\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|x\|$.

## Solution

**Inequality.** For every $x$:
$$\|ABx\|\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|Bx\|\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|x\|.$$
Taking the supremum over $\|x\|=1$: $\|AB\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}$.

**Conclusion.** $\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ is a submultiplicative matrix norm.

@@@ topology-MnR-continuity-determinant.md
---
title: Continuity of the determinant
category: topology/topology-of-mnr
level: l1
difficulty: 2
tags: determinant, continuity, polynomial
date: 2026-11-04
---

## Statement

Show that $\det:M_n(\mathbb{R})\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous.

## Hint

The determinant is a polynomial in the entries.

## Solution

**Polynomial in entries.** By the Leibniz formula,
$$\det(A)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\varepsilon(\sigma)\prod_{i=1}^n a_{i,\sigma(i)}.$$
Each term is a product of continuous coordinate functions; the sum is continuous.

**Conclusion.** $\det$ is continuous, even polynomial in the entries.

@@@ topology-MnR-homeomorphism-quadratic.md
---
title: A homeomorphism of $M_n(\mathbb{R})$
category: topology/topology-of-mnr
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: homeomorphism, matrix map, inverse map
date: 2026-11-04
---

## Statement

Consider $\Phi:M_n(\mathbb{R})\to S_n(\mathbb{R})\times A_n(\mathbb{R})$ defined by $\Phi(A)=(A+A^T,A-A^T)$, where $S_n$ (resp. $A_n$) is the set of symmetric (resp. antisymmetric) matrices. Show $\Phi$ is a homeomorphism.

## Hint

Explicitly find the inverse; both maps are polynomial.

## Solution

**Inverse.** Given $(S,A)$ with $S$ symmetric and $A$ antisymmetric, set $M=\frac{S+A}{2}$. Then $M+M^T=S$, $M-M^T=A$; indeed $M=\frac{S+A}{2}$. So $\Phi^{-1}(S,A)=\frac{S+A}{2}$.

**Continuity.** Both $\Phi$ and $\Phi^{-1}$ are linear maps between finite-dimensional spaces, hence continuous.

**Conclusion.** $\Phi$ is a homeomorphism.

@@@ topology-MnR-summary.md
---
title: Summary of the topology of $M_n(\mathbb{R})$
category: topology/topology-of-mnr
level: lycee
difficulty: 2
tags: summary, matrix topology, M_n(R)
date: 2026-11-04
---

## Statement

Summarize the main topological properties of $M_n(\mathbb{R})$.

## Hint

Review convergence, completeness, compactness, groups.

## Solution

**Identification.** $M_n(\mathbb{R})\cong\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ via entries; all norms are equivalent.

**Convergence.** Entrywise convergence $=$ convergence for any matrix norm.

**Completeness.** $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ is a Banach space.

**Compactness.** Heine–Borel: compact $\iff$ closed and bounded. $O_n$ is compact (closed + bounded); $GL_n$, $SL_n$, $S_n$ are closed or open subsets as appropriate.

**Subgroups.** $GL_n$ is open; $SL_n$, $O_n$, $SO_n$ are closed; $O_n$, $SO_n$ are compact.

**Matrix exponential.** $\exp$ is continuous, even locally Lipschitz.

**Eigenvalues.** Depend continuously on the matrix entries.

**Separability.** $M_n(\mathbb{Q})$ is a countable dense subset.

**Conclusion.** $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ inherits from $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ all its metric properties; the classical matrix groups add rich geometric structure.

@@@ metric-definition.md
---
title: Metric spaces
category: topology/metric
level: l1
difficulty: 1
tags: metric, definition, axioms
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Define a metric space and give two examples.

## Hint

A metric $d:X\times X\to[0,\infty)$ satisfies positivity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality.

## Solution

**Definition.** A metric on $X$ is a map $d:X\times X\to[0,+\infty[$ such that for all $x,y,z\in X$:
1. $d(x,y)=0\iff x=y$;
2. $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$;
3. $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$.

**Examples.**
- Euclidean metric on $\mathbb{R}^n$: $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|_2$.
- Discrete metric: $d(x,y)=0$ if $x=y$, $d(x,y)=1$ otherwise.

**Conclusion.** A metric space is a pair $(X,d)$; the metric encodes distance and topology.

@@@ metric-examples-classical.md
---
title: Classical metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$
category: topology/metric
level: l1
difficulty: 2
tags: Euclidean, Manhattan, sup norm
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Define the Euclidean, Manhattan, and sup metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and compare them.

## Hint

$\|x\|_2\le\|x\|_1\le n\|x\|_2$ and $\|x\|_\infty\le\|x\|_2\le\sqrt n\|x\|_\infty$.

## Solution

**Metrics.**
- Euclidean: $d_2(x,y)=\sqrt{\sum(x_i-y_i)^2}$.
- Manhattan: $d_1(x,y)=\sum|x_i-y_i|$.
- Sup: $d_\infty(x,y)=\max_i|x_i-y_i|$.

**Comparison.** For every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$:
$$\|x\|_\infty\le\|x\|_2\le\|x\|_1\le n\|x\|_\infty.$$

**Conclusion.** These metrics define the same topology (they are equivalent).

@@@ metric-open-ball.md
---
title: Open balls in a metric space
category: topology/metric
level: l1
difficulty: 1
tags: open ball, metric, definition
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Define the open ball $B(a,r)$ in a metric space and show it is open.

## Hint

For $x\in B(a,r)$, use $r-\|x-a\|>0$.

## Solution

**Definition.** $B(a,r)=\{x\in X:d(x,a)<r\}$.

**Openness.** Let $x\in B(a,r)$ and $\rho=r-d(x,a)>0$. For $y\in B(x,\rho)$: $d(y,a)\le d(y,x)+d(x,a)<\rho+d(x,a)=r$.

**Conclusion.** $B(x,\rho)\subseteq B(a,r)$: open balls are open sets.

@@@ metric-convergence.md
---
title: Convergence in metric spaces
category: topology/metric
level: l1
difficulty: 2
tags: convergence, sequences, metric
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Define convergence of a sequence in a metric space and show that limits are unique.

## Hint

Suppose $x_n\to x$ and $x_n\to y$ with $x\neq y$; take $\varepsilon=d(x,y)/2$.

## Solution

**Definition.** $x_n\to x$ iff $d(x_n,x)\to0$.

**Uniqueness.** If $x_n\to x$ and $x_n\to y$, then $d(x,y)\le d(x,x_n)+d(x_n,y)\to0$, so $d(x,y)=0$, hence $x=y$.

**Conclusion.** Limits in metric spaces are unique.

@@@ metric-continuity.md
---
title: Continuity in metric spaces
category: topology/metric
level: l1
difficulty: 2
tags: continuity, epsilon-delta, metric
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Define continuity of $f:X\to Y$ between metric spaces.

## Hint

For all $x_0$, $\forall\varepsilon>0,\exists\delta>0:\ d_X(x,x_0)<\delta\Rightarrow d_Y(f(x),f(x_0))<\varepsilon$.

## Solution

**Definition.** $f$ is continuous at $x_0$ iff $\forall\varepsilon>0,\exists\delta>0:\ d_X(x,x_0)<\delta\Rightarrow d_Y(f(x),f(x_0))<\varepsilon$.

**Global.** $f$ is continuous iff continuous at every point.

**Equivalence.** Equivalent to: $f^{-1}(U)$ open in $X$ for every open $U\subseteq Y$; and to sequential continuity.

**Conclusion.** Continuity has multiple equivalent characterizations in metric spaces.

@@@ metric-compact.md

title: Compactness in metric spaces
category: topology/metric
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: compactness, open cover, sequential
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

State the equivalence between compactness by open covers and sequential compactness in metric spaces.

## Hint

In metric spaces, compact $\Leftrightarrow$ sequentially compact.

## Solution

**Theorem.** For a metric space $X$: compact (every open cover has a finite subcover) $\iff$ every sequence has a convergent subsequence (sequential compactness).

**Key steps.** Sequential compactness implies the space is totally bounded; a totally bounded complete space is compact.

**Conclusion.** Both compactness notions coincide in metric spaces.

@@@ metric-complete.md
---
title: Complete metric spaces
category: topology/metric
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: completeness, Cauchy sequences, examples
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Define completeness and give two examples of complete and two non-complete metric spaces.

## Hint

Complete = every Cauchy sequence converges in the space.

## Solution

**Definition.** A metric space is complete if every Cauchy sequence has a limit in the space.

**Complete.** $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{R}^n$ with Euclidean metric, closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

**Not complete.** $\mathbb{Q}$ (with usual metric: $1,1.4,1.41,\ldots$ converges to $\sqrt2\notin\mathbb{Q}$); $]0,1]$ (sequence $1/n$ is Cauchy but converges to $0\notin]0,1]$).

**Conclusion.** Completeness depends both on the metric and the underlying set.

@@@ metric-equivalence.md

title: Equivalent metrics
category: topology/metric
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: equivalent metrics, same topology, norms
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that the three classical metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equivalent: they define the same topology.

## Hint

Two metrics are topologically equivalent iff each open ball for one contains an open ball for the other.

## Solution

**Bounds.** $\|x\|_\infty\le\|x\|_2\le\sqrt n\|x\|_\infty$, and similar for $\|\cdot\|_1$.

**Consequence.** $B_\infty(a,r/\sqrt n)\subseteq B_2(a,r)\subseteq B_\infty(a,r)$; similarly for $\|\cdot\|_1$.

**Conclusion.** $d_1,d_2,d_\infty$ are topologically equivalent on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

@@@ metric-norm-definition.md

title: Normed spaces
category: topology/metric
level: l1
difficulty: 2
tags: norm, definition, axioms
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Define a norm on a vector space and show that the induced distance is a metric.

## Hint

$\|x\|=0\iff x=0$; $\|\lambda x\|=|\lambda|\|x\|$; triangle inequality.

## Solution

**Axioms.** A norm $\|\cdot\|:E\to[0,+\infty[$ satisfies:
1. $\|x\|=0\iff x=0$;
2. $\|\lambda x\|=|\lambda|\|x\|$;
3. $\|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|$.

**Induced metric.** $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ is a metric: positivity from (1), symmetry from $\|\lambda x\|$ with $\lambda=-1$, triangle from (3).

**Conclusion.** Every normed space is a metric space.

@@@ metric-norm-equivalent.md
---
title: Equivalent norms
category: topology/metric
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: equivalent norms, topology, finite dimension
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that in finite-dimensional spaces, any two norms are equivalent.

## Hint

Work in a basis; the closed unit ball of one norm is compact for the other.

## Solution

**Setup.** Let $\|\cdot\|_1,\|\cdot\|_2$ be two norms on $\mathbb{R}^n$. By compactness of the unit sphere of $\|\cdot\|_1$ (for $\|\cdot\|_2$), the continuous function $\|\cdot\|_1/\|\cdot\|_2$ has a positive minimum $m$ and finite maximum $M$.

**Consequence.** $m\|x\|_2\le\|x\|_1\le M\|x\|_2$.

**Conclusion.** In finite dimension, all norms are equivalent.

**Note.** Fails in infinite dimension (e.g. $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ vs $\|\cdot\|_1$ on $C([0,1])$).

@@@ metric-compact-closed.md
---
title: Compact sets are closed and bounded
category: topology/metric
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: compact, closed, bounded, metric
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that in a metric space, every compact set is closed and bounded.

## Hint

Sequential argument: a limit point outside would contradict compactness; a sequence with no convergent subsequence gives unboundedness.

## Solution

**Closed.** If $x_n\in K$ converges to $x$, sequential compactness gives a convergent subsequence in $K$, so $x\in K$; hence $K$ is closed.

**Bounded.** If $K$ were unbounded, there would exist $(x_n)$ in $K$ with $d(x_0,x_n)\to+\infty$; such a sequence has no convergent subsequence, contradiction.

**Conclusion.** In metric spaces, compact $\Rightarrow$ closed and bounded.

**Note.** The converse holds in $\mathbb{R}^n$ (Heine–Borel) but not in general metric spaces.

@@@ metric-Cauchy.md
---
title: Cauchy sequences
category: topology/metric
level: l1
difficulty: 2
tags: Cauchy, sequences, metric
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Define a Cauchy sequence and show that a convergent sequence is Cauchy.

## Hint

For $\varepsilon>0$, use $d(x_n,x)\to0$ and the triangle inequality.

## Solution

**Definition.** $(x_n)$ is Cauchy if $\forall\varepsilon>0,\ \exists N,\ \forall m,n\ge N,\ d(x_m,x_n)<\varepsilon$.

**Convergent $\Rightarrow$ Cauchy.** If $x_n\to x$, then for $m,n\ge N$, $d(x_m,x_n)\le d(x_m,x)+d(x,x_n)<\varepsilon$.

**Conclusion.** Every convergent sequence is Cauchy.

**Note.** The converse characterizes complete spaces.

@@@ metric-product.md

title: Product metrics
category: topology/metric
level: l1
difficulty: 3

date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

Define a metric on $X\times Y$ in terms of metrics on $X$ and $Y$.

## Hint

$d((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2))=\max(d_X(x_1,x_2),d_Y(y_1,y_2))$.

## Solution

**Definition.** $d((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2))=\max(d_X(x_1,x_2),d_Y(y_1,y_2))$.

**Properties.** Positivity, symmetry, triangle: all inherited component-wise.

**Conclusion.** $X\times Y$ is a metric space; convergence is component-wise.

@@@ metric-Banach.md
---
title: Banach fixed point theorem
category: topology/metric
level: m1
difficulty: 5
tags: Banach, fixed point, contraction
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Let $(X,d)$ be complete and $f:X\to X$ be a contraction ($d(f(x),f(y))\le kd(x,y)$ with $k<1$). Show that $f$ has a unique fixed point and that iterates converge to it.

## Hint

Show $(x_n)$ with $x_{n+1}=f(x_n)$ is Cauchy; use $d(x_{n+1},x_n)\le k^n d(x_1,x_0)$.

## Solution

**Cauchy.** $d(x_{n+1},x_n)\le k^nd(x_1,x_0)$; summing, $d(x_n,x_m)\le\frac{k^n}{1-k}d(x_1,x_0)\to0$.

**Convergence.** Complete: $x_n\to x^*$. Continuity: $f(x^*)=x^*$.

**Uniqueness.** If $f(x^*)=x^*$ and $f(y^*)=y^*$, $d(x^*,y^*)\le kd(x^*,y^*)$, so $d(x^*,y^*)=0$.

**Conclusion.** Banach fixed point theorem holds; iterates converge geometrically.

@@@ metric-Baire.md
---
title: Baire category theorem
category: topology/metric
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: Baire, category, complete
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

State the Baire category theorem for complete metric spaces.

## Hint

In a complete metric space, a countable intersection of dense open sets is dense.

## Solution

**Theorem (Baire).** Let $(X,d)$ be complete. If $(U_n)$ is a sequence of dense open sets, then $\bigcap_nU_n$ is dense.

**Consequence.** A complete metric space is not a countable union of nowhere dense sets.

**Conclusion.** Baire's theorem is a powerful tool in functional analysis (open mapping, closed graph, uniform boundedness).

@@@ metric-completion.md
---
title: Completion of a metric space
category: topology/metric
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: completion, Cauchy, dense embedding
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

State the completion theorem for metric spaces.

## Hint

Every metric space embeds isometrically as a dense subset of a complete metric space.

## Solution

**Theorem.** Given a metric space $(X,d)$, there exists a complete metric space $(\hat X,\hat d)$ and an isometric embedding $i:X\to\hat X$ with dense image. This $(\hat X,\hat d)$ is unique up to isometry.

**Construction.** Take equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences of $X$ (with two sequences equivalent if their pointwise distance tends to $0$).

**Example.** $\mathbb{Q}$ completes to $\mathbb{R}$.

**Conclusion.** Completion fills in "missing limits" in a canonical way.

@@@ metric-norm-examples.md
---
title: Classical normed spaces
category: topology/metric
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: normed spaces, Banach, examples
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

List the classical normed spaces $\ell^p$ and $C([0,1])$.

## Hint

$\ell^p$ sequences with $\sum|x_n|^p<\infty$; $C([0,1])$ with $\sup$-norm.

## Solution

**$\ell^p$ for $1\le p<\infty$.** $\|x\|_p=(\sum|x_n|^p)^{1/p}$.

**$\ell^\infty$.** $\|x\|_\infty=\sup_n|x_n|$.

**$C([0,1])$.** $\|f\|_\infty=\sup_{[0,1]}|f|$.

**Completeness.** All these spaces are Banach (complete normed) spaces.

**Conclusion.** Classical spaces provide examples and counterexamples in functional analysis.

@@@ metric-compact-image.md
---
title: Continuous image of compact
category: topology/metric
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: compact image, continuity, compactness
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that the continuous image of a compact metric space is compact.

## Hint

Sequential: extract a subsequence from a sequence in the image.

## Solution

**Proof.** Let $K$ compact and $f:K\to Y$ continuous. Given a sequence $(f(x_n))$ in $f(K)$, extract a subsequence $x_{n_k}\to x\in K$. Then $f(x_{n_k})\to f(x)\in f(K)$.

**Conclusion.** $f(K)$ is compact; if $Y=\mathbb{R}$, extrema are attained.

@@@ metric-uniform-continuity.md
---
title: Heine–Cantor theorem
category: topology/metric
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: Heine-Cantor, uniform continuity, compact
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

State and prove that continuous maps from a compact metric space are uniformly continuous.

## Hint

Contradiction via sequences.

## Solution

**Theorem.** Continuous $f:K\to Y$ with $K$ compact is uniformly continuous.

**Proof.** Suppose not: $\exists\varepsilon>0$ with $x_n,y_n\in K$, $d(x_n,y_n)\to0$ but $d(f(x_n),f(y_n))\ge\varepsilon$. Compactness of $K$ gives a subsequence $x_{n_k}\to x$; then $y_{n_k}\to x$. Continuity: $f(x_{n_k}),f(y_{n_k})\to f(x)$, contradiction.

**Conclusion.** Heine–Cantor holds in general metric spaces.

@@@ metric-isometry.md
---
title: Isometries between metric spaces
category: topology/metric
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: isometry, metric, distance-preserving
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Define an isometry and show it is injective.

## Hint

If $f(x)=f(y)$, apply $d(f(x),f(y))=d(x,y)$.

## Solution

**Definition.** $f:X\to Y$ is an isometry if $d_Y(f(x),f(y))=d_X(x,y)$ for all $x,y$.

**Injectivity.** $f(x)=f(y)\Rightarrow d_Y(f(x),f(y))=0\Rightarrow d_X(x,y)=0\Rightarrow x=y$.

**Conclusion.** Every isometry is injective; if surjective, it is an isometric isomorphism.

@@@ metric-non-compact-closed-bounded.md
---
title: Closed bounded sets need not be compact
category: topology/metric
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: counterexample, compactness, infinite dimension
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Give an example of a closed bounded set that is not compact in a metric space.

## Hint

In $\ell^2$, the closed unit ball is closed and bounded but not compact.

## Solution

**Counterexample.** In $\ell^2$ (space of square-summable sequences with $\|\cdot\|_2$), the closed unit ball $\overline B(0,1)$ is closed and bounded. But the sequence $(e_n)$ of standard basis vectors is at pairwise distance $\sqrt2$, so has no convergent subsequence.

**Conclusion.** In infinite dimension, closed bounded $\not\Rightarrow$ compact.

**Note.** Riesz's theorem: the closed unit ball of a normed space is compact iff the space is finite-dimensional.

@@@ topology-Rn-open-ball.md
---
title: Open balls in $\mathbb{R}^n$
category: topology/topology-of-rn
level: l1
difficulty: 1
tags: open ball, Euclidean norm, definition
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Define the open ball $B(a,r)$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and show it is an open set.

## Hint

For $x\in B(a,r)$, take $\rho=r-\|x-a\|>0$ and use the triangle inequality.

## Solution

**Definition.** $B(a,r)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\|x-a\|<r\}$.

**Openness.** Let $x\in B(a,r)$ and $\rho=r-\|x-a\|>0$. For $y\in B(x,\rho)$: $\|y-a\|\le\|y-x\|+\|x-a\|<\rho+\|x-a\|=r$. So $B(x,\rho)\subseteq B(a,r)$.

**Conclusion.** Open balls are open sets.

@@@ topology-Rn-open-definition.md
---
title: Open sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$
category: topology/topology-of-rn
level: l1
difficulty: 1
tags: open sets, definition, ball
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

State the definition of an open set in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and give two examples.

## Hint

$U$ is open iff every point of $U$ has a small ball contained in $U$.

## Solution

**Definition.** $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is open iff for all $x\in U$ there is $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subseteq U$.

**Examples.** $\mathbb{R}^n$ itself, open balls, $\{x:x_1>0\}$ (open half-space).

**Counterexample.** The closed ball $\overline B(a,r)$ is not open (its boundary points fail the condition).

**Conclusion.** Openness is defined pointwise via balls.

@@@ topology-Rn-closed.md

title: Closed sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$

## Statement

Define a closed set in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and give two examples.

## Hint

Closed = complement open.

## Solution

**Definition.** $F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is closed iff $\mathbb{R}^n\setminus F$ is open.

**Examples.** Closed ball $\overline B(a,r)=\{x:\|x-a\|\le r\}$; spheres $\{x:\|x-a\|=r\}$; hyperplanes.

**Conclusion.** Closed sets are complements of open ones.

@@@ topology-Rn-union-intersection.md
---
title: Stability of open and closed sets
category: topology/topology-of-rn
level: l1
difficulty: 2
tags: unions, intersections, stability
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that arbitrary unions and finite intersections of open sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are open; dual properties for closed sets.

## Hint

For finite intersections, take the minimum of radii. For closed sets, use De Morgan's laws.

## Solution

**Union.** If $x\in\bigcup U_i$, pick $i_0$ with $x\in U_{i_0}$; use the ball around $x$ inside $U_{i_0}$.

**Finite intersection.** With $x\in U_1\cap\cdots\cap U_n$, take $r=\min_i r_i>0$ where $B(x,r_i)\subseteq U_i$.

**Closed sets.** By De Morgan: arbitrary intersections and finite unions of closed sets are closed.

**Conclusion.** The topology is stable under the expected operations.

@@@ topology-Rn-interior-closure.md
---
title: Interior, closure, boundary
category: topology/topology-of-rn
level: l1
difficulty: 2
tags: interior, closure, boundary
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Define the interior, closure and boundary of $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, and compute them for $A=B(a,r)$ (open ball).

## Hint

$\overline{A}$ is the smallest closed set containing $A$; boundary $=\overline A\setminus\mathring A$.

## Solution

**Definitions.**
- Interior: union of open subsets of $A$.
- Closure: intersection of closed sets containing $A$; equivalently $A$ plus its limit points.
- Boundary: $\overline A\setminus\mathring A$.

**For $A=B(a,r)$.**
- Interior: $A$ itself (it is open).
- Closure: $\overline B(a,r)=\{x:\|x-a\|\le r\}$.
- Boundary: sphere $\{x:\|x-a\|=r\}$.

**Conclusion.** For an open ball, boundary is the sphere, closure is the closed ball.

@@@ topology-Rn-limit-points.md
---
title: Limit points in $\mathbb{R}^n$
category: topology/topology-of-rn
level: l1
difficulty: 2
tags: limit points, sequences, closure
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that $x$ is in the closure of $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ iff there is a sequence $(x_k)$ in $A$ with $x_k\to x$.

## Hint

Use $\varepsilon$-balls and sequential characterisation.

## Solution

**$\Leftarrow$.** If $x_k\to x$ with $x_k\in A$, every ball around $x$ contains a $x_k$. So $x$ is a limit point of $A$; $x\in\overline A$.

**$\Rightarrow$.** If $x\in\overline A$, for each $k$ pick $x_k\in A\cap B(x,1/k)$; such a ball always meets $A$ by definition of closure.

**Conclusion.** Closure equals the set of limits of sequences in $A$.

## Statement

State the Heine–Borel theorem in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and give examples.

## Hint

In $\mathbb{R}^n$, compact = closed + bounded.

## Solution

**Theorem.** $K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is compact iff $K$ is closed and bounded.

**Examples.**
- Compact: closed ball $\overline B(0,1)$, the cube $[0,1]^n$, spheres.
- Non-compact: open ball $B(0,1)$ (not closed), hyperplane (not bounded).

**Conclusion.** Compactness in $\mathbb{R}^n$ = closed and bounded.

State the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

## Hint

Every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence.

## Solution

**Theorem.** Every bounded sequence in $\mathbb{R}^n$ has a convergent subsequence.

**Link to compactness.** If $K$ is compact, every sequence in $K$ has a subsequence converging in $K$ (sequential compactness).

@@@ topology-Rn-connected.md

title: Connectedness in $\mathbb{R}^n$
category: topology/topology-of-rn
level: l1
difficulty: 3

date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

Define connectedness and path-connectedness of subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$, and show that any convex set is path-connected.

## Hint

For convex $C$, the segment between any two points lies in $C$.

## Solution

**Definitions.**
- $A$ is connected if no separation $A=U\cup V$ with $U,V$ nonempty open, disjoint.
- $A$ is path-connected if any two points are joined by a continuous path in $A$.

**Convex $\Rightarrow$ path-connected.** For $x,y\in C$ convex, the segment $t\mapsto(1-t)x+ty$, $t\in[0,1]$, lies in $C$.

**Conclusion.** Convex sets are path-connected (hence connected).

@@@ topology-Rn-continuity-open.md
---
title: Continuity and open preimages
category: topology/topology-of-rn
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: continuity, open preimages, multivariable
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ is continuous iff $f^{-1}(U)$ is open for every open $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m$.

## Hint

Copy the one-dimensional proof, replacing intervals by balls.

## Solution

**$\Leftarrow$.** Given $x_0$ and $\varepsilon>0$, the ball $U=B(f(x_0),\varepsilon)$ is open. So $f^{-1}(U)$ is open; it contains $x_0$, hence $B(x_0,\delta)\subseteq f^{-1}(U)$. So $\|f(x)-f(x_0)\|<\varepsilon$ for $\|x-x_0\|<\delta$.

**$\Rightarrow$.** Given open $U$ and $x_0\in f^{-1}(U)$, $f(x_0)\in U$ gives $\varepsilon>0$ with $B(f(x_0),\varepsilon)\subseteq U$; continuity gives $\delta$ with $f(B(x_0,\delta))\subseteq U$.

**Conclusion.** Continuity is equivalent to the preimage of open sets being open.

@@@ topology-Rn-boundary-sphere.md

title: Boundary of a ball
category: topology/topology-of-rn
level: l1

tags: boundary, sphere, ball
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Compute the boundary of the closed ball $\overline B(a,r)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$.

## Hint

Boundary = closure $\setminus$ interior. The closed ball is its own closure; its interior is the open ball.

## Solution

**Closure.** $\overline B(a,r)$ is closed, so its closure is itself.

**Interior.** $\mathring{\overline B}=B(a,r)$: any boundary point fails to have a ball inside the closed ball.

**Boundary.** $\overline{B(a,r)}\setminus B(a,r)=\{x:\|x-a\|=r\}$.

**Conclusion.** The boundary is the sphere $S(a,r)=\{x:\|x-a\|=r\}$.

@@@ topology-Rn-limit-not-continuity.md
---
title: Continuity versus iterated limits
category: topology/topology-of-rn
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: iterated limits, continuity, subtleties
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that $f(x,y)=\dfrac{xy}{x^2+y^2}$ (with $f(0,0)=0$) has iterated limits $0$ along both axes but no limit at the origin.

## Hint

Compute limits along $y=0$ and $x=0$, then along $y=x$.

## Solution

**Iterated limits.** $f(x,0)=0$, $f(0,y)=0$: so $\lim_{x\to0}\lim_{y\to0}f=\lim_{y\to0}\lim_{x\to0}f=0$.

**Diagonal.** Along $y=x$: $f(x,x)=\frac12$, so the limit along this path is $1/2$.

**Conclusion.** Iterated limits exist and coincide, but the two-dimensional limit does not: $f$ is not continuous at the origin.

@@@ topology-Rn-compactness-image.md

## Statement

Show that if $K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is compact and $f:K\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $f$ attains its maximum and minimum on $K$.

## Hint

$f(K)$ is compact in $\mathbb{R}$, hence closed and bounded; contains its supremum and infimum.

## Solution

**Image compact.** $f(K)$ is compact in $\mathbb{R}$ (continuous image of compact is compact).

**Extrema.** $f(K)$ is closed and bounded in $\mathbb{R}$: it contains its supremum $M$ and infimum $m$. So there exist $x_{\max}, x_{\min}\in K$ with $f(x_{\max})=M$, $f(x_{\min})=m$.

**Conclusion.** Continuous functions on compact sets attain their extrema.

@@@ topology-Rn-uniform-continuity.md
---
title: Heine–Cantor in $\mathbb{R}^n$
category: topology/topology-of-rn
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: uniform continuity, Heine-Cantor, compactness
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

State Heine–Cantor theorem for $\mathbb{R}^n$ and outline its proof.

## Hint

Argue by contradiction using sequential compactness.

## Solution

**Theorem.** A continuous $f:K\to\mathbb{R}^m$ on a compact $K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is uniformly continuous.

**Proof.** Assume not: $\exists\varepsilon>0$ with $\|x_k-y_k\|\to0$ but $\|f(x_k)-f(y_k)\|\ge\varepsilon$. Compactness gives a subsequence $x_{k_j}\to x$. Then $y_{k_j}\to x$ too. Continuity: $f(x_{k_j})\to f(x)$ and $f(y_{k_j})\to f(x)$, contradiction.

**Conclusion.** Heine–Cantor holds in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

@@@ topology-Rn-baire.md
---
title: Baire category theorem for $\mathbb{R}^n$
category: topology/topology-of-rn
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: Baire, complete metric, category
date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

State Baire's theorem for $\mathbb{R}^n$ and explain its use for the existence of functions continuous nowhere differentiable.

## Hint

$\mathbb{R}^n$ is a complete metric space; the set of continuous functions is meager in the space of all functions, but the set of nowhere-differentiable ones is residual.

## Solution

**Baire's theorem.** In a complete metric space, a countable intersection of dense open sets is dense.

**Application.** In the space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ with the uniform norm, the set of nowhere-differentiable functions is a dense $G_\delta$ (residual) — hence non-empty (in fact, "typical").

**Conclusion.** Baire's theorem forces the existence of highly irregular but continuous functions.

@@@ topology-Rn-isometry.md
---
title: Isometries of $\mathbb{R}^n$
category: topology/topology-of-rn
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: isometry, Euclidean, rigid motion
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that every isometry $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ is of the form $f(x)=Qx+b$ with $Q$ orthogonal.

## Hint

Translate to assume $f(0)=0$; then $Q=f$ preserves the norm; use the polarization identity to show $Q$ is linear.

## Solution

**Norm preservation.** Since $f$ is an isometry and $f(0)=0$, $\|f(x)\|=\|x\|$.

**Linear.** Polarization identity: $\langle f(x),f(y)\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$. This linearises $f$: for $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$, $f(\lambda x)=\lambda f(x)$ and $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$.

**Orthogonal.** $Q=f$ satisfies $Q^TQ=I$.

**Conclusion.** Any isometry of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is an orthogonal transformation plus a translation.

@@@ topology-Rn-homeomorphism-ball-cube.md

## Statement

Show that the unit ball $B(0,1)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and the open cube $]-1,1[^n$ are homeomorphic.

## Hint

Use a scaling by the sup-norm: $T(x)=x/\|x\|_\infty\cdot\|x\|_2$ (or directly $T(x)=\frac{\|x\|_2}{\|x\|_\infty}x$ when $x\neq0$).

## Solution

**Map.** Define $T(x)=\frac{\|x\|_2}{\|x\|_\infty}x$ for $x\neq0$, $T(0)=0$. This maps the cube $\|x\|_\infty<1$ onto the ball $\|x\|_2<1$.

**Inverse.** The inverse is $T^{-1}(y)=\frac{\|y\|_\infty}{\|y\|_2}y$, continuous.

**Conclusion.** Ball and cube are homeomorphic.

@@@ topology-R-open-interval.md

title: Open intervals are open sets
category: topology/topology-of-r

difficulty: 1
tags: open sets, open intervals, definition
date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

Show that any open interval $]a,b[$ (with $a<b$) is an open set of $\mathbb{R}$.

## Hint

For any $x\in]a,b[$, take $r=\min(x-a,b-x)>0$; then $]x-r,x+r[\subseteq]a,b[$.

## Solution

**Radius.** Let $x\in]a,b[$ and $r=\min(x-a,b-x)>0$. Then for any $y\in]x-r,x+r[$: $y<x+r\le b$ and $y>x-r\ge a$. So $y\in]a,b[$.

**Conclusion.** Every $x\in]a,b[$ has a neighbourhood inside $]a,b[$; the interval is open.

@@@ topology-R-open-ball.md

## Statement

For $a\in\mathbb{R}$ and $r>0$, describe the open ball $B(a,r)$ and show it is an open set.

@@@ topology-R-union-open.md
---
title: Arbitrary unions of open sets
category: topology/topology-of-r
level: l1
difficulty: 2
tags: unions, open sets, arbitrary
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that an arbitrary union of open sets of $\mathbb{R}$ is open.

## Hint

For $x$ in the union, it belongs to at least one open set $U_i$; use the open ball around $x$ inside $U_i$.

## Solution

**Proof.** Let $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ be open and $x\in\bigcup_i U_i$. Pick $i_0$ with $x\in U_{i_0}$. Since $U_{i_0}$ is open, there is $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subseteq U_{i_0}\subseteq\bigcup_i U_i$.

**Conclusion.** $\bigcup_i U_i$ is open.

**Remark.** Finite intersections of open sets are open, but infinite intersections may fail: $\bigcap_{n\ge1}]-\frac1n,\frac1n[=\{0\}$, not open.

title: Finite intersections of open sets
category: topology/topology-of-r

---

## Statement

Show that the intersection of finitely many open sets of $\mathbb{R}$ is open.

## Hint

For $x\in U_1\cap\cdots\cap U_n$, take the minimum of the radii from each $U_i$.

## Solution

**Proof.** Let $U_1,\ldots,U_n$ be open and $x\in\bigcap U_i$. For each $i$, there is $r_i>0$ with $B(x,r_i)\subseteq U_i$. Let $r=\min(r_1,\ldots,r_n)>0$. Then $B(x,r)\subseteq\bigcap U_i$.

**Conclusion.** The intersection is open.

## Statement

Show that $[a,b]$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}$.

## Hint

Its complement $]-\infty,a[\cup]b,+\infty[$ is a union of open sets.

## Solution

**Complement.** $\mathbb{R}\setminus[a,b]=]-\infty,a[\cup]b,+\infty[$, a union of open sets, hence open.

**Conclusion.** $[a,b]$ is closed.

@@@ topology-R-closed-definition.md

title: Closed sets
category: topology/topology-of-r
level: l1
difficulty: 2
tags: closed sets, complement, definition
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Define a closed set in $\mathbb{R}$ and give two examples and one counterexample.

## Hint

Closed = complement is open.

## Solution

**Definition.** $F\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is closed iff $\mathbb{R}\setminus F$ is open.

**Examples.** $\emptyset$, $\mathbb{R}$, $[0,1]$, singletons $\{a\}$.

**Counterexample.** $]0,1]$ is neither open nor closed: it is not open (0 is a boundary point) and its complement $]-\infty,0]\cup]1,+\infty[$ is not open.

**Conclusion.** Some sets are neither open nor closed.

@@@ topology-R-boundary.md
---
title: Interior, closure, boundary
category: topology/topology-of-r
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: interior, closure, boundary
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

For $A=]0,1]\cup\{2\}$, compute the interior, closure, and boundary of $A$.

## Hint

$\mathring A$ = union of open subsets of $A$; $\overline A$ = smallest closed set containing $A$; $\partial A=\overline A\setminus\mathring A$.

## Solution

**Interior.** $\mathring A=]0,1[$: $1$ is not interior (every ball around $1$ hits the complement), $2$ is not interior (isolated).

**Closure.** $\overline A=[0,1]\cup\{2\}$: the limit points of $]0,1]$ are in $[0,1]$; $2$ is already in $A$.

**Boundary.** $\partial A=\{0,1,2\}$.

**Conclusion.** Interior $]0,1[$, closure $[0,1]\cup\{2\}$, boundary $\{0,1,2\}$.

@@@ topology-R-limits.md

title: Limit points

level: l1

tags: limit points, accumulation, closure
date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

Define a limit point of a set $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ and describe the limit points of $A=\{1/n:n\ge1\}$.

## Hint

$x$ is a limit point if every neighbourhood of $x$ meets $A\setminus\{x\}$.

## Solution

**Definition.** $x$ is a limit point of $A$ if $\forall\varepsilon>0$, $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\cap(A\setminus\{x\})\neq\emptyset$.

**Limit points of $A$.** Only $0$: any $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood of $0$ contains infinitely many $1/n$; other points are isolated.

**Conclusion.** $A'=\{0\}$; the closure is $\overline A=A\cup\{0\}$.

@@@ topology-R-compact.md

title: Compact sets in $\mathbb{R}$
category: topology/topology-of-r

## Statement

State the Heine–Borel theorem and give two examples of compact and two non-compact sets.

## Hint

A subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is compact iff it is closed and bounded.

## Solution

**Theorem (Heine–Borel).** $K\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is compact iff $K$ is closed and bounded.

**Compact.** $[0,1]$, $\{0\}\cup\{1/n:n\ge1\}$.

**Non-compact.** $]0,1[$ (not closed), $[0,+\infty[$ (not bounded).

**Conclusion.** Compactness = closed + bounded in $\mathbb{R}$.

@@@ topology-R-open-cover.md
---
title: The Borel–Lebesgue property
category: topology/topology-of-r
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: compactness, open cover, finite subcover
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Recall the definition of compactness by open covers and show that $[0,1]$ has the Borel–Lebesgue property.

## Hint

Standard proof: assume a cover with no finite subcover, bisect, iterate, get contradiction.

## Solution

**Definition.** $K$ is compact if every open cover of $K$ admits a finite subcover.

**Proof sketch for $[0,1]$.** Suppose $(U_i)$ is an open cover with no finite subcover. Bisect $[0,1]$: one half also has no finite subcover. Iterate to get nested intervals $I_n$ of length $2^{-n}$, each requiring infinitely many $U_i$. Their intersection is a single point $x\in[0,1]$, which lies in some $U_{i_0}$. For $n$ large, $I_n\subseteq U_{i_0}$ — contradiction.

**Conclusion.** $[0,1]$ is compact.

@@@ topology-R-connected.md
---
title: Connected subsets of $\mathbb{R}$
category: topology/topology-of-r
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: connectedness, intervals, IVT
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that the connected subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are exactly the intervals.

## Hint

If $A$ has a gap, split $A\cap]-\infty,c[$ and $A\cap]c,+\infty[$. Conversely, if $A$ is an interval, any separation would contradict the IVT for the identity.

## Solution

**Interval connected.** If $A$ is an interval and $A=U\cup V$ with $U,V$ disjoint nonempty open in $A$, take $u\in U$, $v\in V$, WLOG $u<v$. Since $A$ is an interval, $[u,v]\subseteq A$. The sets $U\cap[u,v]$ and $V\cap[u,v]$ give a separation of $[u,v]$, contradiction with connectedness of intervals.

**Non-interval disconnected.** If $a<b<c$ with $a,c\in A$, $b\notin A$, then $A\cap]-\infty,b[$ and $A\cap]b,+\infty[$ separate $A$.

**Conclusion.** Connected subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ = intervals.

@@@ topology-R-continuity-characterisation.md
---
title: Continuity via open preimages
category: topology/topology-of-r
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: continuity, open preimages, topological definition
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous iff $f^{-1}(U)$ is open for every open $U$.

## Hint

$(\Leftarrow)$: apply to $U=]f(x_0)-\varepsilon,f(x_0)+\varepsilon[$. $(\Rightarrow)$: use the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition.

## Solution

**$\Leftarrow$.** Given $x_0$ and $\varepsilon>0$, the ball $U=]f(x_0)-\varepsilon,f(x_0)+\varepsilon[$ is open, so $f^{-1}(U)$ is open. It contains $x_0$, hence contains $B(x_0,\delta)\subseteq f^{-1}(U)$. So $|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon$ for $|x-x_0|<\delta$.

**$\Rightarrow$.** Given open $U$ and $x_0\in f^{-1}(U)$, $f(x_0)\in U$ gives $\varepsilon>0$ with $B(f(x_0),\varepsilon)\subseteq U$. Continuity provides $\delta>0$ with $B(x_0,\delta)\subseteq f^{-1}(U)$.

**Conclusion.** Continuity is topological.

@@@ topology-R-cantor-set.md
---
title: The Cantor set is compact
category: topology/topology-of-r
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: Cantor set, compactness, closed
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that the Cantor set $K$ (intersection of nested triadic sets) is compact.

## Hint

$K$ is the intersection of closed bounded sets.

## Solution

**Construction.** $K=\bigcap_n K_n$ with $K_0=[0,1]$, $K_{n+1}$ removing the middle thirds of each interval of $K_n$.

**Closed.** Each $K_n$ is a union of closed intervals, hence closed; the intersection is closed.

**Bounded.** $K\subseteq[0,1]$.

**Conclusion.** $K$ is closed and bounded, hence compact (Heine–Borel).

**Remark.** $K$ is also uncountable, perfect, and has empty interior.

@@@ topology-R-open-dense.md

title: Dense sets
category: topology/topology-of-r
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: dense, rationals, irrationals
date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

Show that $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ are both dense in $\mathbb{R}$.

## Hint

Between any two reals there is a rational, and between any two reals there is an irrational.

## Solution

**$\mathbb{Q}$ dense.** For $a<b$ reals, pick $n$ with $1/n<b-a$; some $k/n\in]a,b[$.

**$\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ dense.** Given $a<b$, take a rational $q\in]a,b[$; then $q+\frac{\sqrt2}{n}\in]a,b[$ for large $n$ is irrational.

**Conclusion.** Both $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ are dense in $\mathbb{R}$.

@@@ topology-R-baire.md
---
title: Baire category theorem for $\mathbb{R}$
category: topology/topology-of-r
level: m1
difficulty: 5
tags: Baire, category, dense G-delta
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

State and prove that $\mathbb{R}$ is not a countable union of nowhere dense sets.

## Hint

Assume $\mathbb{R}=\bigcup F_n$; construct nested intervals avoiding each $F_n$.

## Solution

**Statement (Baire).** $\mathbb{R}$ is not a countable union of nowhere dense sets.

**Proof.** Suppose $\mathbb{R}=\bigcup_n F_n$ with each $F_n$ nowhere dense. Construct nested closed intervals $I_n$ with $I_n\cap F_n=\emptyset$ and $\mathrm{diam}(I_n)\le2^{-n}$. Their intersection is a point $x\notin\bigcup F_n$ — contradiction.

**Conclusion.** $\mathbb{R}$ is of second Baire category, in particular uncountable.

**Remark.** A dense $G_\delta$ (e.g. irrationals) is residual; its complement is meager.

@@@ topology-R-limit-superior.md

## Statement

Compute $\limsup$ and $\liminf$ of $u_n=(-1)^n\left(1+\frac1n\right)$.

## Hint

## Solution

**Even.** $u_{2k}=1+\frac{1}{2k}\to1$.

**Odd.** $u_{2k+1}=-(1+\frac{1}{2k+1})\to-1$.

@@@ topology-R-compact-char.md

## Statement

State the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem and explain its link with compactness of $[0,1]$.

## Hint

Every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence.

## Solution

**Theorem (Bolzano–Weierstrass).** Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence.

**Link.** If $K\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is compact (closed and bounded), every sequence in $K$ is bounded, so has a convergent subsequence; its limit lies in $K$ since $K$ is closed.

@@@ topology-R-accumulation.md

title: Accumulation points of $\mathbb{Q}$
category: topology/topology-of-r
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: accumulation, rationals, density
date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

Show that every real number is an accumulation point of $\mathbb{Q}$.

## Hint

Use density of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$.

## Solution

**Proof.** Let $x\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Since $\mathbb{Q}$ is dense, there is $q\in\mathbb{Q}\cap(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)$. If $q\neq x$, done; if $q=x$, take another rational in the smaller ball $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\setminus\{x\}$.

**Conclusion.** Every real number is an accumulation point of $\mathbb{Q}$; $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}=\mathbb{R}$.

@@@ continuity-summary.md
---
title: Summary of continuity
category: calculus/multivariable/continuity
level: l2
difficulty: 2
tags: summary, continuity
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Summarize the key points of continuity for several variables.

## Hint

Review methods and theorems.

## Solution

**Basic.** Polynomials and quotients of continuous functions (where denominator nonzero) are continuous.

**Continuity at a point.** Show $f(x,y)\to f(x_0,y_0)$; use bounding, polar coordinates, or the squeeze theorem.

**Discontinuity.** Exhibit two paths with different limits, or a path where the limit diverges or doesn't exist.

**Notable counterexamples.** $f(x,y)=\frac{xy}{x+y}$ at origin, $\frac{x^2y}{x^4+y^2}$ (discontinuous despite radial limits), $\sin(1/r^2)$.


**Key theorems.** Continuous image of compact is compact; continuous on compact is uniformly continuous (Heine–Cantor); norm and projections are continuous.

**Conclusion.** Continuity in several variables is subtler than in one variable; multiple paths must be considered.

@@@ continuity-discontinuous-two-paths.md

date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

Show that $f(x,y)=\dfrac{xy}{x+y}$ (with $f(0,0)=0$) is not continuous at the origin.

## Hint

Along $y=ax$ with $a\neq-1$, $f(x,ax)=\frac{ax}{1+a}$, whose limit depends on $a$.

## Solution

**Dependence on $a$.** On $y=ax$, $f(x,ax)=\frac{ax}{1+a}$. As $x\to0$, this tends to $0$ for each $a$... 

**Second family.** Along $y=ax+bx^2$ with $a=-1$, $b\neq0$: $f(x,-x+bx^2)=\frac{x(-x+bx^2)}{bx^2}=\frac{-x+bx^2}{bx}=\frac{-1}{b}+x$, tending to $-1/b$, which varies with $b$.

**Conclusion.** Limits differ along different paths; $f$ is not continuous at the origin.

## Statement

Show that the continuous image of a compact set is compact, and deduce the existence of extrema.

## Hint

## Solution

@@@ continuity-heine-cantor.md
---
title: Heine–Cantor theorem
category: calculus/multivariable/continuity
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: uniform continuity, compact, Heine
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

State and prove that a continuous function on a compact set is uniformly continuous.

## Hint

Argue by contradiction: assume $\exists\varepsilon>0$ such that $\forall\delta>0$ there are $x,y$ with $\|x-y\|<\delta$ and $\|f(x)-f(y)\|\ge\varepsilon$.

## Solution

**Contradiction.** If $f$ is not uniformly continuous, there is $\varepsilon>0$ and sequences $x_n,y_n$ in $K$ with $\|x_n-y_n\|\to0$ but $\|f(x_n)-f(y_n)\|\ge\varepsilon$.

**Subsequence.** By compactness, extract $x_{n_k}\to x\in K$. Then $y_{n_k}\to x$ too. Continuity gives $f(x_{n_k})\to f(x)$ and $f(y_{n_k})\to f(x)$, contradicting the gap.

**Conclusion.** $f$ is uniformly continuous on $K$.

@@@ constrained-critical-two-points.md

## Statement

Find and classify the critical points of $f(x,y)=4x+2y-x^2-y^2-2x^3$.

## Hint

Solve $f_x=4-2x-6x^2=0$, $f_y=2-2y=0$; then use the Hessian at each point.

## Solution

**Critical points.** $f_y=0\Rightarrow y=1$. $4-2x-6x^2=0\Rightarrow 3x^2+x-2=0\Rightarrow x=-1$ or $x=2/3$. Points: $A=(-1,1)$, $B=(2/3,1)$.

## Statement

Find and classify the critical point of $f(x,y)=xy+x^3y^2$.

## Hint

$f_x=y(1+3x^2y)$, $f_y=x(1+2x^2y)$.

## Solution

**System.** $y(1+3x^2y)=0$ and $x(1+2x^2y)=0$. Only solution: $(0,0)$.

**Hessian at $(0,0)$.** $f_{xx}=6xy^2$, $f_{xy}=1+6x^2y$, $f_{yy}=2x^3$; $H(0,0)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

**Determinant.** $\det H=-1<0$: saddle point.

**Conclusion.** The only critical point $(0,0)$ is a saddle.

## Statement

Find and classify the critical point of $f(x,y,z)=yz+zx-xy$.

## Hint

$\nabla f=(z-y,z-x,y+x)$; Hessian is constant.

## Solution

**Critical point.** Setting all partials to zero gives $x=y=z=0$.

**Hessian.**
$$H=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&1\\-1&0&1\\1&1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$

**Determinant.** $\det H=-2$, $\operatorname{tr}H=0$. Eigenvalues can't be all positive (product $-2$) or all negative (sum $0$).

**Conclusion.** The origin is a saddle point.

## Statement

Find the extrema of $f(x,y)=3x-y$ under the constraint $x^2+y^2=5$.

## Hint

$\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g$ with $g=x^2+y^2-5$.

## Solution

**Lagrange system.**
$$3=2\lambda x,\quad -1=2\lambda y,\quad x^2+y^2=5.$$

**Solve.** $x=3/(2\lambda)$, $y=-1/(2\lambda)$, so $y=-x/3$. Then $x^2+x^2/9=5\Rightarrow x^2=9/2\Rightarrow x=\pm3/\sqrt2$.

**Points.** $A=(3/\sqrt2,-1/\sqrt2)$, $B=(-3/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2)$.

**Values.** $f(A)=5\sqrt2$ (maximum), $f(B)=-5\sqrt2$ (minimum).

**Conclusion.** Maximum $5\sqrt2$ at $A$, minimum $-5\sqrt2$ at $B$.

## Statement

Maximize the volume $V=xyz$ of a rectangular box under the constraint $2(xy+yz+zx)=A$ (fixed surface area).

## Hint

By symmetry the optimum is the cube. Apply Lagrange to confirm.

## Solution

**Lagrange.** $\nabla(xyz)=\lambda\nabla(2(xy+yz+zx))$:
$$yz=2\lambda(y+z),\quad xz=2\lambda(x+z),\quad xy=2\lambda(x+y).$$

## Statement

Using Lagrange multipliers, prove that $x+y\le\sqrt{2(x^2+y^2)}$.

## Hint

Maximize $x+y$ under $x^2+y^2=1$; multiply by the radius.

## Solution

**Lagrange.** $1=2\lambda x$, $1=2\lambda y$, so $x=y$. On the unit circle, $x=y=1/\sqrt2$, giving maximum $\sqrt2$.

**Scaling.** For any $(x,y)\neq(0,0)$ with $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, $(x/r,y/r)$ is on the unit circle, so $x+y\le\sqrt2\,r$.

@@@ constrained-summary.md
---
title: Summary of constrained optimization
category: calculus/multivariable/constrained-optimisation
level: lycee
difficulty: 2
tags: summary, constrained optimization
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Summarize the key methods for constrained optimization.

## Hint

Review critical points, Hessian, Lagrange, boundary.

## Solution

**Unconstrained critical points.**
- Solve $\nabla f=0$.
- Classify via the Hessian: positive definite (min), negative definite (max), indefinite (saddle).

**Lagrange multipliers.** For $f$ under $g=0$: $\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g$, plus the constraint.

**Boundary.** Parameterize or restrict $f$ to the boundary surface; combine with interior results.

**Compact sets.** If the set is compact, global extrema exist; check interior, boundary, and corners.

**KKT for inequalities.** For $g\le0$: Lagrange with nonnegativity conditions.

**Examples.** Circles, lines, ellipsoids, quadratics, multi-constraint problems.

**Conclusion.** Constrained optimization reduces to finding critical points of the Lagrangian and evaluating on boundaries.

## Statement

Compute $\displaystyle\int_C(x+y)\,ds$ where $C$ is the segment from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$.

## Hint

Parametrize $\gamma(t)=(t,t)$, $t\in[0,1]$, and $ds=\|\gamma'(t)\|\,dt$.

## Solution

**Parametrization.** $\gamma(t)=(t,t)$, $\gamma'(t)=(1,1)$, $\|\gamma'(t)\|=\sqrt2$.

**Integral.**
$$\int_0^1(t+t)\sqrt2\,dt=2\sqrt2\int_0^1 t\,dt=\sqrt2.$$

**Conclusion.** $\int_C(x+y)\,ds=\sqrt2$.

## Statement

Find a potential for $\vec F(x,y)=(e^x\cos y,\,-e^x\sin y)$.

## Solution

@@@ vector-line-fundamental-theorem.md
---
title: Fundamental theorem for line integrals
category: calculus/multivariable/vector-calculus
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: fundamental theorem, line integral, potential
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

State the fundamental theorem for line integrals: if $\vec F=\nabla\phi$, then $\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r=\phi(B)-\phi(A)$.

## Hint

Apply the univariate chain rule along a parametrization.

## Solution

**Proof.** Let $\gamma(t)$, $t\in[a,b]$, parametrize $C$ from $A$ to $B$. Then
$$\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r=\int_a^b\nabla\phi(\gamma(t))\cdot\gamma'(t)\,dt=\int_a^b\frac{d}{dt}[\phi(\gamma(t))]\,dt=\phi(B)-\phi(A).$$

**Conclusion.** For conservative fields, the integral only depends on endpoints.

## Statement

Compute the flux of $\vec F=(x,y,z)$ through the sphere $S$ of radius $R$ centered at the origin, oriented outward.

## Hint

$\iint_S\vec F\cdot\vec n\,dS=\iiint_V\operatorname{div}\vec F\,dV$.

## Solution

**Divergence.** $\operatorname{div}\vec F=1+1+1=3$.

**Theorem.** Flux $=3\cdot\text{Vol}(V)=3\cdot\frac43\pi R^3=4\pi R^3$.

**Conclusion.** Flux $=4\pi R^3$.

## Statement

State Green's reciprocity identity: for functions $u,v$ on a domain $D$ with boundary $\partial D$,
$$\iint_D(u\Delta v-v\Delta u)=\oint_{\partial D}\left(u\frac{\partial v}{\partial n}-v\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\right)ds.$$

## Hint

Apply the divergence theorem to $\vec F=u\nabla v-v\nabla u$.

## Solution

**Divergence.** $\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)=u\Delta v+\nabla u\cdot\nabla v$. Similarly for $v\nabla u$. Difference: $u\Delta v-v\Delta u$.

**Apply.** Divergence theorem gives the boundary identity.

**Conclusion.** Green's reciprocity identity follows from the divergence theorem.

## Statement

## Solution

**Lower path.** $\gamma_1(t)=(t,t)$, $t\in[0,1]$. Contribution $\frac12\int_0^1(t\cdot1-t\cdot1)\,dt=0$.

**Upper path.** $\gamma_2(t)=(t,t^2)$ from $t=1$ to $0$ (reverse). Compute $\frac12\int_{1}^{0}(t\cdot2t-t^2\cdot1)\,dt=\frac12\int_1^0 t^2\,dt=\frac12\cdot(-\frac13)=-\frac16$; absolute value $\frac16$.

Wait, sign issue: total area should be positive. Let me just compute $|x^2-x|$ directly: area $=\int_0^1(x-x^2)\,dx=\frac12-\frac13=\frac16$.

**Conclusion.** Area $=1/6$.

## Statement

Show that $\vec F=(yz,xz,xy)$ is conservative and find a potential.

## Solution

**Conclusion.** $\vec F=\nabla(xyz)$.

@@@ multint-polar-annulus.md

## Statement

Compute $\displaystyle I=\iint_D\frac{dx\,dy}{x^2+y^2+xy}$ where $D=\{4\le x^2+y^2\le16\}$.

## Hint

Polar: $x^2+y^2+xy=r^2(1+\cos\theta\sin\theta)$.

## Solution

**Polar.** $I=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_2^4\frac{r\,dr\,d\theta}{r^2(1+\cos\theta\sin\theta)}=\int_2^4\frac{dr}{r}\cdot\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{1+\cos\theta\sin\theta}$.

**Radial.** $\int_2^4 dr/r=\ln2$.

**Angular integral.** Using $\cos\theta\sin\theta=\frac12\sin 2\theta$ and $t=\theta-\pi/2$, substitution $u=\tan t$:
$$J=\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{1+\frac12\sin2\theta}=2\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\frac{dt}{1-\frac12\sin2t}=2\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\frac{du}{(u-\frac12)^2+\frac34}=\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt3}.$$

**Total.** $I=\frac{4\pi\ln2}{\sqrt3}$.

**Conclusion.** $I=\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt3}\ln2$.

## Statement

$$\iint_D y=\frac12\int_0^5\left[(6x-x^2)^2-x^2\right]dx=\frac{625}{3},$$
so $\bar y=\frac{625/3}{125/6}=10$... wait, careful: $\bar y=625/(3\cdot125/6)=10$? Check numeric: $625\cdot 6/(3\cdot125)=10$. But the geometric answer is $5$. Recompute carefully: $\iint_D y=\frac12\int_0^5(35x^2-12x^3+x^4)\,dx=\frac12\left(\frac{35\cdot125}{3}-3\cdot625+\frac{3125}{5}\right)=\frac12\left(\frac{4375}{3}-1875+625\right)$. Compute: $\frac{4375}{3}-1250=\frac{4375-3750}{3}=\frac{625}{3}$. So $\iint_D y=\frac{625}{6}$, and $\bar y=\frac{625/6}{125/6}=5$.

**Conclusion.** Centroid at $(5/2,5)$.

@@@ multint-fubini-trick.md
---
title: The Fubini trick
category: calculus/multivariable/multiple-integrals
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: Fubini, double integral, iterated
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Compute $\displaystyle I=\int_0^1\frac{\ln(1+x)}{1+x^2}\,dx$ using Fubini.

## Hint

Write $\ln(1+x)=\int_0^1\frac{x\,dy}{1+xy}$ and apply Fubini, then use symmetry in $x,y$.

## Solution

**Write as double integral.**
$$I=\int_0^1\int_0^1\frac{x}{(1+x^2)(1+xy)}\,dy\,dx.$$

**Symmetry.** Reversing $x\leftrightarrow y$:
$$2I=\int_0^1\int_0^1\frac{x+y}{(1+x^2)(1+y^2)}\,dx\,dy.$$

**Separate.**
$$2I=\left(\int_0^1\frac{x}{1+x^2}\,dx\right)\left(\int_0^1\frac{1}{1+y^2}\,dy\right)+\left(\int_0^1\frac{1}{1+x^2}\,dx\right)\left(\int_0^1\frac{y}{1+y^2}\,dy\right).$$
Both equal $\frac12\ln2\cdot\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi\ln2}{8}$. So $2I=\frac{\pi\ln2}{4}$, $I=\frac{\pi\ln2}{8}$.

**Conclusion.** $I=\frac{\pi\ln2}{8}$.

@@@ multint-polar-annular-region.md
---
title: Polar region between two circles
category: calculus/multivariable/multiple-integrals
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: polar, circle, region between circles
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Compute $\displaystyle I=\iint_D\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\,dx\,dy$ where $D=\{x^2+y^2\ge2y,\ x^2+y^2\le1\}$.

## Hint

In polar: $x^2+y^2\le1$ gives $r\le1$; $x^2+y^2\ge2y$ gives $r\ge2\sin\theta$. Determine the range of $\theta$.

## Solution

**Polar.** $\sin\theta\le1/2$ for the two-disk overlap; the region splits into $\theta\in[0,\pi/6]$, $[5\pi/6,\pi]$, $[\pi,2\pi]$.

**Compute each piece.**
- $I_1$ over $[\pi,2\pi]$, $0\le r\le1$: $I_1=\int_\pi^{2\pi}\int_0^1r^2\,dr\,d\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$.
- $I_2$ over $[0,\pi/6]$, $2\sin\theta\le r\le1$: $I_2=\frac{\pi}{18}+\sqrt3-\frac{16}{9}$.
- $I_3$ over $[5\pi/6,\pi]$, by symmetry $I_3=I_2$.

**Sum.** $I=\frac{\pi}{3}+\frac{2\pi}{18}+2\sqrt3-\frac{32}{9}=\frac{4\pi-32}{9}+2\sqrt3$.

**Conclusion.** $I=\frac{4\pi-32}{9}+2\sqrt3$.

@@@ multint-triple-with-sin.md
---
title: Triple integral with sine
category: calculus/multivariable/multiple-integrals
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: triple integral, sine, simplex
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Compute $\displaystyle \iiint_V\frac{\sin x}{\pi-x-y}\,dx\,dy\,dz$ where $V=\{x,y,z\ge0,\ x+y+z\le\pi\}$.

## Hint

Integrate in $z$ first: the inner integral is $\sin x$.

## Solution

**Iterated.**
$$I=\int_0^\pi\int_0^{\pi-x}\int_0^{\pi-x-y}\frac{\sin x}{\pi-x-y}\,dz\,dy\,dx.$$

**Inner in $z$.** $z$ from $0$ to $\pi-x-y$: the inner integral equals $\sin x$.

**In $y$.** $\int_0^{\pi-x}\sin x\,dy=(\pi-x)\sin x$.

**In $x$.** $I=\int_0^\pi(\pi-x)\sin x\,dx=\pi\int_0^\pi\sin x-\int_0^\pi x\sin x=\pi\cdot2-\pi=\pi$.

**Conclusion.** $I=\pi$.

@@@ multint-triple-cube.md

title: Triple integral over a cube
category: calculus/multivariable/multiple-integrals
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: cube, triple integral, iterated
date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

Compute $\displaystyle I=\iiint_{[0,1]^3}\frac{dx\,dy\,dz}{(x+y+z+1)^3}$.

## Hint

Integrate in $x$ first: $\int_0^1\frac{dx}{(x+c)^3}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{c^2}-\frac{1}{(c+1)^2}\right)$.

## Solution

**Inner in $x$.** $\frac12\left(\frac{1}{(y+z+1)^2}-\frac{1}{(y+z+2)^2}\right)$.

**In $y$.** $\frac12\left(\frac{1}{z+1}-\frac{2}{z+2}+\frac{1}{z+3}\right)$.

**In $z$.** $I=\frac12\left(\ln2-2\ln\frac32+\ln\frac43\right)=\frac{5\ln2-3\ln3}{2}$.

**Conclusion.** $I=\frac{5\ln2-3\ln3}{2}$.

@@@ multint-triple-simplex-p3.md
---
title: Triple integral over a simplex with cube
category: calculus/multivariable/multiple-integrals
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: simplex, triple integral, iterated
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Compute $\displaystyle I=\iiint_D\frac{dx\,dy\,dz}{(x+y+z+1)^3}$ where $D=\{x,y,z\ge0,\ x+y+z\le1\}$.

## Hint

Order $z,y,x$: $0\le z\le1-x-y$.

## Solution

**Inner in $z$.**
$$\int_0^{1-x-y}\frac{dz}{(x+y+z+1)^3}=\frac{1}{2(x+y+1)^2}-\frac18.$$

**In $y$.** $\frac12\int_0^{1-x}\frac{dy}{(x+y+1)^2}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac12\right)$, minus $\frac18(1-x)$.

**In $x$.** 
$$I=\frac12\int_0^1\left(\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac12\right)dx-\frac18\cdot\frac12=\frac12\left(\ln2-\frac12\right)-\frac{1}{16}.$$

**Result.** $I=\frac12\ln2-\frac{5}{16}$.

**Conclusion.** $I=\frac12\ln2-\frac{5}{16}$.

@@@ multint-spherical-volume.md

title: Volume of a sphere by triple integral
category: calculus/multivariable/multiple-integrals

tags: spherical coordinates, volume, sphere
date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

Compute the volume of the ball $B_R=\{x^2+y^2+z^2\le R^2\}$ using spherical coordinates.

## Hint

$x=r\sin\varphi\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\varphi\sin\theta$, $z=r\cos\varphi$; Jacobian $r^2\sin\varphi$.

## Solution

**Spherical.** $0\le r\le R$, $0\le\varphi\le\pi$, $0\le\theta\le2\pi$.

**Jacobian.** $r^2\sin\varphi$.

**Compute.**
$$V=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^R r^2\sin\varphi\,dr\,d\varphi\,d\theta=2\pi\cdot2\cdot\frac{R^3}{3}=\frac{4\pi R^3}{3}.$$

**Conclusion.** $V=\frac{4\pi R^3}{3}$.

@@@ multint-spherical-radial.md
---
title: Spherical coordinates with a radial integrand
category: calculus/multivariable/multiple-integrals
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: spherical coordinates, radial, integration
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Compute $\displaystyle I=\iiint_{B_R}e^{-\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}}\,dx\,dy\,dz$ where $B_R$ is the ball of radius $R$.

## Hint

Spherical: integrand $e^{-r}$, Jacobian $r^2\sin\varphi$.

## Solution

**Setup.**
$$I=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^R e^{-r}r^2\sin\varphi\,dr\,d\varphi\,d\theta=4\pi\int_0^R r^2e^{-r}\,dr.$$

**Compute.** $\int_0^R r^2e^{-r}\,dr=2-(R^2+2R+2)e^{-R}$ (two integrations by parts).

**Result.** $I=4\pi[2-(R^2+2R+2)e^{-R}]$.

**Conclusion.** $I=4\pi\left(2-(R^2+2R+2)e^{-R}\right)$.

## Statement

@@@ multint-summary.md
---
title: Summary of multiple integrals
category: calculus/multivariable/multiple-integrals
level: l1
difficulty: 2
tags: summary, multiple integrals
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Summarize key tools for multiple integrals.

## Hint

Review Fubini, change of variables, polar, spherical, cylindrical.

## Solution

**Fubini.** Iterated integration on product domains.

**Change of variables.** $dx\,dy\to|J|\,du\,dv$; $|J|$ is the Jacobian determinant.

**Polar.** $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$, $dx\,dy=r\,dr\,d\theta$.

**Cylindrical.** $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$, $z=z$, $dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz$.

**Spherical.** $x=r\sin\varphi\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\varphi\sin\theta$, $z=r\cos\varphi$, $dV=r^2\sin\varphi\,dr\,d\varphi\,d\theta$.

**Applications.** Volumes, centroids, masses with variable density, Gaussian integrals.

**Conclusion.** Multiple integrals reduce to iterated integrals via Fubini, and change of variables exploits symmetries to simplify computations.

@@@ partial-derivatives-chain-rule.md

title: Chain rule for a composition

date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

Let $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ and $\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$. Compute $\frac{d}{dt}f(\gamma(t))$ two ways.

## Hint

Direct composition gives $f(\gamma(t))=1$; the chain rule gives $\nabla f(\gamma(t))\cdot\gamma'(t)$.

## Solution

**Direct.** $f(\gamma(t))=\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1$, derivative $0$.

**Chain rule.** $\nabla f=(2x,2y)$, $\gamma'(t)=(-\sin t,\cos t)$. So $\nabla f(\gamma(t))\cdot\gamma'(t)=2\cos t(-\sin t)+2\sin t\cos t=0$.

**Conclusion.** Both methods give $0$: $f$ is constant on the circle.

@@@ partial-derivatives-chain-general.md
---
title: General chain rule
category: calculus/multivariable/partial-derivatives
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: chain rule, composition, multivariable
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Let $f(u,v)=u^2v$ and $u(x,y)=x+y$, $v(x,y)=xy$. Compute $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(u,v)$ and $\frac{\partial}{\partial y}f(u,v)$.

## Hint

Apply the chain rule:
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=f_u u_x+f_v v_x.$$

## Solution

**Partial derivatives of $f$.** $f_u=2uv$, $f_v=u^2$.

**Chain rule for $\partial_x$.**
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=2uv\cdot1+u^2\cdot y=2(x+y)(xy)+y(x+y)^2=(x+y)(2xy+y(x+y)).$$

**Chain rule for $\partial_y$.**
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=2uv\cdot1+u^2\cdot x=2(x+y)(xy)+x(x+y)^2=(x+y)(2xy+x(x+y)).$$

**Conclusion.** Both partial derivatives are polynomials in $x,y$.

@@@ partial-derivatives-higher-order.md
---
title: Second-order partial derivatives
category: calculus/multivariable/partial-derivatives
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: higher order, Schwarz, second derivatives
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Let $f(x,y)=x^3y^2+xy$. Compute all four second-order partial derivatives and check Schwarz's theorem.

## Hint

Differentiate $f_x$ and $f_y$ once more; compare $f_{xy}$ and $f_{yx}$.

## Solution

**First derivatives.** $f_x=3x^2y^2+y$, $f_y=2x^3y+x$.

**Second derivatives.** $f_{xx}=6xy^2$, $f_{yy}=2x^3$, $f_{xy}=6x^2y+1$, $f_{yx}=6x^2y+1$.

**Conclusion.** $f_{xy}=f_{yx}$: Schwarz's theorem holds (the mixed partials are equal because $f$ is $C^2$).

@@@ partial-derivatives-schwarz.md
---
title: Schwarz's theorem
category: calculus/multivariable/partial-derivatives
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: Schwarz theorem, mixed partials, symmetry
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

State Schwarz's theorem and give an example where mixed partials differ at a point.

## Hint

Schwarz requires continuity of second partials. Counterexample: $f(x,y)=xy(x^2-y^2)/(x^2+y^2)$.

## Solution

**Theorem.** If $f$ is $C^2$ in a neighbourhood of a point, then $f_{xy}=f_{yx}$ there.

**Counterexample.** $f(x,y)=xy(x^2-y^2)/(x^2+y^2)$ for $(x,y)\neq(0,0)$, $f(0,0)=0$. Then $f_{xy}(0,0)=-1$ but $f_{yx}(0,0)=1$.

**Diagnosis.** The second partials are not continuous at $(0,0)$.

**Conclusion.** Schwarz's theorem requires $C^2$ regularity; the counterexample fails this hypothesis.

@@@ partial-derivatives-differentiability.md
---
title: Differentiability of a piecewise function

level: l1

tags: differentiability, continuity, piecewise

## Statement

Let
$$f(x,y)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{xy}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}&\text{if }(x,y)\neq(0,0),\\0&\text{if }(x,y)=(0,0).\end{cases}$$
Show that $f$ is continuous at $(0,0)$ and compute its partial derivatives there.

Bound $|xy|\le(x^2+y^2)/2$ and use the definition of partials.

**Conclusion.** $f$ is continuous with $f_x(0,0)=f_y(0,0)=0$. (However, $f$ is not differentiable at $(0,0)$: check along $y=x$.)

@@@ partial-derivatives-differential.md

title: The differential
category: calculus/multivariable/partial-derivatives

tags: differential, linearization, approximation
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Let $f(x,y)=x^3+y^3$. Compute the differential at $(1,2)$ and use it to approximate $f(1.01,1.99)$.

## Hint

$df=f_x(a,b)\,dx+f_y(a,b)\,dy$ with $dx=0.01$, $dy=-0.01$.

## Solution

**Exact value.** $1.01^3+1.99^3\approx1.0303+7.8806=8.9109$, very close.

**Conclusion.** Linear approximation gives $\approx8.91$.

For $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$, describe the level curves and show that the gradient is orthogonal to them.

## Hint

Level curve $f=c$ is a circle; parameterize and differentiate.

## Solution

**Level curves.** $f=c$ is the circle $x^2+y^2=c$ of radius $\sqrt c$ (for $c>0$).

**Parameterization.** $\gamma(t)=(\sqrt c\cos t,\sqrt c\sin t)$; $\gamma'(t)=\sqrt c(-\sin t,\cos t)$ is tangent.

**Gradient.** $\nabla f=2(x,y)=2\gamma(t)$, radial and orthogonal to $\gamma'(t)$:
$$(2\sqrt c\cos t,2\sqrt c\sin t)\cdot(-\sqrt c\sin t,\sqrt c\cos t)=0.$$

**Conclusion.** $\nabla f$ is orthogonal to the level curves; it points in the direction of fastest increase of $f$.

@@@ partial-derivatives-implicit.md
---
title: Implicit differentiation
category: calculus/multivariable/partial-derivatives
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: implicit differentiation, Implicit Function Theorem
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

The curve $x^2+y^2=1$ defines $y$ implicitly as a function of $x$ near $(1/2,\sqrt3/2)$. Compute $y'(x)$ by implicit differentiation.

## Hint

Differentiate $x^2+y(x)^2=1$ with respect to $x$.

## Solution

**Differentiation.** $2x+2y(x)y'(x)=0$.

**Solve.** $y'(x)=-x/y(x)$.

**At $x=1/2$.** $y=\sqrt3/2$, so $y'(1/2)=-\frac{1/2}{\sqrt3/2}=-1/\sqrt3$.

**Conclusion.** $y'(1/2)=-1/\sqrt3$, consistent with the geometric interpretation of a tangent to the circle.

@@@ partial-derivatives-inverse-function.md
---
title: Inverse function theorem (illustration)
category: calculus/multivariable/partial-derivatives
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: inverse function theorem, Jacobian, local invertibility
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Let $F(x,y)=(e^x\cos y,e^x\sin y)$. Compute the Jacobian matrix at $(0,0)$ and check the inverse function theorem.

## Hint

Jacobian columns: derivatives with respect to $x$ and $y$.

## Solution

**Partial derivatives.** $\partial_x F=(e^x\cos y,e^x\sin y)$, $\partial_y F=(-e^x\sin y,e^x\cos y)$.

**Jacobian at $(0,0)$.** $J_F(0,0)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.

**Conclusion.** $\det J=1\neq0$, so the inverse function theorem applies: $F$ is a local diffeomorphism near $(0,0)$.

@@@ partial-derivatives-jacobian.md
---
title: The Jacobian matrix
category: calculus/multivariable/partial-derivatives
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: Jacobian, matrix, vector-valued functions
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Let $F(x,y,z)=(x\cos y,\, y\sin z,\, xyz)$. Compute the Jacobian matrix $J_F$.

## Hint

Each column is the derivative with respect to one variable.

## Solution

**Partial derivatives.**
- $\partial_x F=(\cos y,\,0,\,yz)$
- $\partial_y F=(-x\sin y,\,\sin z,\,xz)$
- $\partial_z F=(0,\,y\cos z,\,xy)$

**Jacobian matrix.**
$$J_F=\begin{pmatrix}\cos y&-x\sin y&0\\0&\sin z&y\cos z\\yz&xz&xy\end{pmatrix}.$$

**Conclusion.** $J_F$ is $3\times3$.

@@@ partial-derivatives-jacobian-composition.md

title: Jacobian of a composition
category: calculus/multivariable/partial-derivatives
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: Jacobian, composition, chain rule
date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

State the chain rule in matrix form: $J_{F\circ G}(x)=J_F(G(x))\cdot J_G(x)$.

## Hint

This is the multivariable analogue of $(f\circ g)'=f'(g)\cdot g'$.

## Solution

**Statement.** If $G:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ and $F:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^p$ are differentiable, then
$$J_{F\circ G}(x)=J_F(G(x))\cdot J_G(x).$$

**Application.** Computing derivatives of composite functions via matrix multiplication.

**Conclusion.** The Jacobian of a composition is the product of Jacobians.

@@@ partial-derivatives-clairaut.md

## Statement

State Clairaut's theorem (Schwarz) and give a sufficient condition for $f_{xy}=f_{yx}$.

## Hint

Continuity of second partials is sufficient.

## Solution

**Theorem.** If $f$ has continuous second partial derivatives in a neighbourhood of a point, then $f_{xy}=f_{yx}$ at that point.

**Sufficient condition.** $f$ is $C^2$.

**Conclusion.** Mixed partials commute under $C^2$ regularity.

@@@ partial-derivatives-optimisation-first.md
---
title: Finding critical points
category: calculus/multivariable/partial-derivatives
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: critical points, stationary, gradient
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Find the critical points of $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2-2x-4y$.

## Hint

Set both partial derivatives to zero.

## Solution

**Gradient.** $\nabla f=(2x-2,2y-4)$.

**Critical point.** $2x-2=0\Rightarrow x=1$; $2y-4=0\Rightarrow y=2$. So $(1,2)$.

**Nature.** Rewrite $f=(x-1)^2+(y-2)^2-5$: minimum at $(1,2)$.

**Conclusion.** The unique critical point is $(1,2)$, a global minimum.

@@@ partial-derivatives-hessian.md
---
title: The Hessian matrix
category: calculus/multivariable/partial-derivatives
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: Hessian, second derivatives, quadratic form
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Compute the Hessian of $f(x,y)=x^2+4xy+3y^2$ at $(0,0)$ and classify the critical point.

## Hint

The Hessian is the matrix of second partials; classify via its eigenvalues.

## Solution

**Partial derivatives.** $f_x=2x+4y$, $f_y=4x+6y$; $f_{xx}=2$, $f_{yy}=6$, $f_{xy}=4$.

**Hessian.** $H=\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\4&6\end{pmatrix}$.

**Eigenvalues.** $\det(H-\lambda I)=(2-\lambda)(6-\lambda)-16=\lambda^2-8\lambda-4$; roots $\lambda=4\pm2\sqrt5$. One positive, one negative.

**Conclusion.** The origin is a saddle point (Hessian is indefinite).

@@@ partial-derivatives-taylor-2.md
