## Statement

Negate the statement: $\forall\varepsilon>0,\ \exists N\in\mathbb{N},\ \forall n\ge N,\ |u_n-\ell|<\varepsilon$. Interpret the negation.

## Hint

Apply the negation rules layer by layer: $\neg\forall\to\exists$, $\neg\exists\to\forall$, and negate the innermost inequality.

## Solution

**Negation.**
$$\exists\varepsilon>0,\ \forall N\in\mathbb{N},\ \exists n\ge N,\ |u_n-\ell|\ge\varepsilon.$$

**Interpretation.** There is some $\varepsilon>0$ such that, no matter how far we go, some term of the sequence is at distance $\ge\varepsilon$ from $\ell$. This is exactly the definition of "$(u_n)$ does not converge to $\ell$".

@@@ quantifiers-order-matters.md

## Statement

Compare the truth values of:
- $P_1$: $\forall x\in\mathbb{R},\ \exists y\in\mathbb{R},\ y>x$;
- $P_2$: $\exists y\in\mathbb{R},\ \forall x\in\mathbb{R},\ y>x$.

In $P_1$, $y$ may depend on $x$; in $P_2$, one $y$ must work for all $x$.

## Solution

**$P_2$ is false.** No real number is larger than every real.

@@@ quantifiers-uniqueness.md

## Statement

Write "there exists a unique real $x$ such that $x^2=0$" in formal notation, and prove it.

## Hint

Use $\exists!$ for "there exists a unique".

## Solution

**Notation.** $\exists! x\in\mathbb{R},\ x^2=0$.

**Proof.**
- *Existence.* $x=0$ satisfies $x^2=0$.
- *Uniqueness.* If $x^2=0$ then $x=0$.

**Conclusion.** The statement holds.

@@@ quantifiers-negation-unique.md

## Statement

## Hint

$\neg(\exists!x,\ P(x))$ means: either no $x$ satisfies $P$, or at least two do.

## Solution

**Negation.** Either $\nexists x,\ x^2=1$ or $\exists x\neq y$ with $x^2=y^2=1$.

**Concretely.** $x=1$ and $x=-1$ both satisfy $x^2=1$, so the original statement is false. The negation holds.

@@@ quantifiers-double-negation.md
---
title: Double negation
category: logic/quantifiers
level: lycee
difficulty: 1
tags: double negation, logic, equivalence
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that $\neg\neg P\equiv P$.

## Hint

Build a truth table.

## Solution

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
  \hline
  P & \neg P & \neg\neg P \\
  \hline
  \text{T} & \text{F} & \text{T} \\
  \text{F} & \text{T} & \text{F} \\
  \hline
\end{array}
$$

The third column equals the first.

**Conclusion.** $\neg\neg P\equiv P$.

@@@ quantifiers-de-morgan-quantifiers.md
---
title: De Morgan's laws for quantifiers
category: logic/quantifiers
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: De Morgan, quantifiers, negation
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

State and prove the two De Morgan laws for quantifiers:
$$\neg(\forall x,\ P(x))\equiv\exists x,\ \neg P(x),\qquad \neg(\exists x,\ P(x))\equiv\forall x,\ \neg P(x).$$

## Hint

For the first: if not all satisfy $P$, some fails $P$. For the second: if no $x$ satisfies $P$, all fail $P$.

## Solution

**First law.** $\neg(\forall x,\ P(x))$ means "it is not the case that every $x$ satisfies $P$", i.e. some $x$ does not satisfy $P$: $\exists x,\ \neg P(x)$.

**Second law.** $\neg(\exists x,\ P(x))$ means "no $x$ satisfies $P$", i.e. every $x$ fails $P$: $\forall x,\ \neg P(x)$.

**Conclusion.** Both laws hold; they generalize De Morgan's laws for connectives.

@@@ quantifiers-epsilon-delta.md
---
title: The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition of limit
category: logic/quantifiers
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: epsilon-delta, quantifiers, limit
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Write the definition of $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=\ell$ using quantifiers, and write its negation.

## Hint

The positive definition uses $\forall\varepsilon>0,\ \exists\delta>0,\ \forall x,\ \ldots$

## Solution

**Definition.**
$$\forall\varepsilon>0,\ \exists\delta>0,\ \forall x\in\mathbb{R},\ (0<|x-a|<\delta\Rightarrow|f(x)-\ell|<\varepsilon).$$

**Negation.**
$$\exists\varepsilon>0,\ \forall\delta>0,\ \exists x\in\mathbb{R},\ (0<|x-a|<\delta\ \text{and}\ |f(x)-\ell|\ge\varepsilon).$$

**Conclusion.** The negation expresses "there is some $\varepsilon$ such that, however small $\delta$ is, some $x$ nearby violates the bound".

Write the formal definition of "$(u_n)$ converges to $\ell$", then express what it means for $(u_n)$ to be unbounded.

@@@ quantifiers-alternation-depth.md
---
title: Alternation depth of quantifiers
category: logic/quantifiers
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: quantifier alternation, depth, complexity
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Give an example of a statement with quantifier alternation $\forall\exists\forall\exists$ and explain why the order cannot be permuted.

## Hint

Consider $\forall a\in\mathbb{N},\ \exists b\in\mathbb{N},\ \forall c\in\mathbb{N},\ \exists d\in\mathbb{N},\ ad-bc=1$.

## Solution

**Example.** $\forall a,\ \exists b,\ \forall c,\ \exists d,\ ad-bc=1$.

**Meaning.** For every $a$, there is $b$ such that, for every $c$, there is $d$ with $ad-bc=1$.

**Permutation.** If we tried $\exists d,\ \forall a,\ \exists b,\ \forall c,\ \ldots$, the single $d$ would have to work for all $a$ and $c$ simultaneously, which is much stronger.

**Conclusion.** Alternation depth controls expressiveness; the order of quantifiers cannot generally be changed.

@@@ quantifiers-conditional-scope.md
---
title: Scope of quantifiers
category: logic/quantifiers
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: scope, quantifiers, ambiguity
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Explain the difference between:
- $P_1$: $\forall x,\ P(x)\Rightarrow Q$;
- $P_2$: $\forall x,\ (P(x)\Rightarrow Q)$.

## Hint

Consider whether $Q$ depends on $x$.

## Solution

**$P_1$.** $\forall x,\ P(x)\Rightarrow Q$: if all $x$ satisfy $P$, then $Q$. Here $Q$ does not depend on $x$; the quantifier applies only to $P(x)$.

**$P_2$.** $\forall x,\ (P(x)\Rightarrow Q)$: for every $x$, if $P(x)$ then $Q$. Each implication is quantified separately.

**Example.** $P(x)$: "$x$ is a counterexample"; $Q$: "the conjecture is false". $P_1$: "if all are counterexamples, the conjecture is false". $P_2$: "every counterexample makes the conjecture false".

**Conclusion.** Scope matters: $\forall x,\ P(x)\Rightarrow Q$ and $\forall x,\ (P(x)\Rightarrow Q)$ differ in meaning.

@@@ quantifiers-double-quantifier-proof.md

## Statement

Show that $\exists a\in\mathbb{R},\ \forall x\in\mathbb{R},\ x^2+ax+a>0$? Determine for which $a$ this holds.

## Hint

The quadratic is positive everywhere iff its discriminant is negative.

## Solution

@@@ quantifiers-induction-quantifier.md
---
title: Quantifiers in induction proofs
category: logic/quantifiers
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: induction, quantifiers, base case
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Express the principle of induction using quantifiers.

## Hint

$\forall P:\ (\text{Base}\land\text{Step})\Rightarrow\forall n\ge n_0,\ P(n)$.

## Solution

**Principle.** For any predicate $P$ on integers,
$$[P(n_0)\land\forall n\ge n_0,\ (P(n)\Rightarrow P(n+1))]\Rightarrow\forall n\ge n_0,\ P(n).$$

**Conclusion.** Induction is a second-order axiom: quantified over predicates $P$.

**Remark.** In first-order arithmetic, induction is an axiom scheme: one instance per definable predicate.

@@@ quantifiers-free-and-bound.md
---
title: Free and bound variables
category: logic/quantifiers
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: free variable, bound variable, quantifier
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

In $\forall x,\ (P(x)\land Q(y))$, identify free and bound variables.

## Hint

Variables under the scope of a quantifier are bound; others are free.

## Solution

**Bound.** $x$ is bound by $\forall x$.

**Free.** $y$ is free (not quantified).

**Closure.** If we add $\exists y$ at the front, then $y$ becomes bound too.

@@@ quantifiers-change-of-variable.md
---
title: Renaming bound variables
category: logic/quantifiers
level: l1

date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that $\forall x,\ P(x)$ and $\forall y,\ P(y)$ are equivalent ($\alpha$-conversion).

## Hint

Both express that every element of the domain satisfies $P$.

## Solution

**Meaning.** $\forall x,\ P(x)$: every element satisfies $P$. $\forall y,\ P(y)$: same.

**Conclusion.** Renaming bound variables preserves meaning; this is called $\alpha$-conversion.

**Caution.** Renaming a free variable is not allowed; e.g. $\forall x,\ P(x,y)$ is not equivalent to $\forall x,\ P(x,z)$ in general.

@@@ quantifiers-absorption.md
---
title: Quantifier absorption
category: logic/quantifiers
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: quantifier absorption, vacuous quantifier
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

When is $\forall x,\ P$ equivalent to $P$, where $P$ does not involve $x$?

## Hint

If $P$ is independent of $x$, the quantifier is vacuous.

## Solution

**Claim.** If $x$ does not occur free in $P$, then $\forall x,\ P\equiv P$ and $\exists x,\ P\equiv P$.

**Justification.** $\forall x,\ P$ asserts "$P$ holds for every $x$"; if $P$ doesn't depend on $x$, this is just "$P$ holds" (assuming the domain is nonempty). Similarly for $\exists$.

**Conclusion.** Vacuous quantifiers can be dropped.

@@@ quantifiers-logical-equivalence.md
---
title: Logical equivalence of quantified statements
category: logic/quantifiers
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: equivalence, quantifiers, distribution
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Is $\forall x,\ (P(x)\land Q(x))$ equivalent to $(\forall x,\ P(x))\land(\forall x,\ Q(x))$?

## Hint

Show both implications.

## Solution

**Forward.** If every $x$ satisfies both $P$ and $Q$, then every $x$ satisfies $P$, and every $x$ satisfies $Q$.

**Backward.** If every $x$ satisfies $P$, and every $x$ satisfies $Q$, then for any $x$, both $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ hold.

**Conclusion.** Yes, the equivalence holds.

**Contrast.** $\forall x,\ (P(x)\lor Q(x))$ is *not* equivalent to $(\forall x,\ P(x))\lor(\forall x,\ Q(x))$.

difficulty: 4
tags: distribution, counterexample, quantifier
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that $\forall x,\ (P(x)\lor Q(x))$ is not equivalent to $(\forall x,\ P(x))\lor(\forall x,\ Q(x))$.

## Hint

Find a domain and predicates where the first is true but the second is false.

## Solution

**Counterexample.** Domain $\{1,2\}$. $P(x)$: "$x=1$". $Q(x)$: "$x=2$".

**First.** $\forall x,\ P(x)\lor Q(x)$: at $x=1$, $P$ true; at $x=2$, $Q$ true. So true.

**Second.** $\forall x,\ P(x)$ is false ($x=2$ fails). $\forall x,\ Q(x)$ is false ($x=1$ fails). So the disjunction is false.

**Conclusion.** Distribution of $\forall$ over $\lor$ fails in general.

**Dual.** $\exists x,\ (P(x)\land Q(x))$ does not distribute as $\exists x,\ P(x)\land\exists x,\ Q(x)$.

@@@ quantifiers-prenex-normal-form.md
---
title: Prenex normal form
category: logic/quantifiers
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: prenex form, quantifiers, normal form
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Put $\neg(\forall x,\ \exists y,\ P(x,y))$ into prenex normal form.

## Hint

Apply the negation rules.

## Solution

**Negation.** $\neg(\forall x,\ \exists y,\ P(x,y))\equiv\exists x,\ \neg(\exists y,\ P(x,y))\equiv\exists x,\ \forall y,\ \neg P(x,y)$.

**Conclusion.** The prenex form is $\exists x,\ \forall y,\ \neg P(x,y)$.

**General.** Every first-order formula is equivalent to one in prenex form (all quantifiers at the front).

@@@ quantifiers-summary.md
---
title: Summary of quantifiers and negation
category: logic/quantifiers
level: lycee
difficulty: 2
tags: summary, quantifiers, negation
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Summarize the key facts about quantifiers.

## Hint

Review definitions, negation rules, and order.

## Solution

**Definitions.**
- $\forall x,\ P(x)$: $P$ holds for all $x$.
- $\exists x,\ P(x)$: some $x$ satisfies $P$.
- $\exists! x,\ P(x)$: exactly one $x$ satisfies $P$.

**Negation.**
- $\neg\forall x,\ P(x)\equiv\exists x,\ \neg P(x)$.
- $\neg\exists x,\ P(x)\equiv\forall x,\ \neg P(x)$.
- $\neg\exists!x,\ P(x)$: no $x$ or at least two $x$ satisfy $P$.

**Order.** $\forall\exists$ does not imply $\exists\forall$ in general.

**Vacuous truth.** $\forall x\in\emptyset,\ P(x)$ is true.

**Conclusion.** Quantifiers are the backbone of mathematical statements; negation and order are critical for correct reasoning.

@@@ logic-direct-proof.md
---
title: Direct proof
category: logic/proof-techniques
level: lycee
difficulty: 1
tags: direct proof, implication, even odd
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove directly: if $n$ is an even integer, then $n^2$ is even.

## Hint

Write $n=2k$ for some integer $k$, then compute $n^2$.

## Solution

**Hypothesis.** $n$ even means $n=2k$ for some $k\in\mathbb{Z}$.

**Computation.** $n^2=(2k)^2=4k^2=2(2k^2)$.

**Conclusion.** Since $2k^2\in\mathbb{Z}$, $n^2$ is even.

@@@ logic-contrapositive.md
---
title: Proof by contraposition
category: logic/proof-techniques
level: lycee
difficulty: 2
tags: contrapositive, implication, odd
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove: if $n^2$ is odd, then $n$ is odd.

## Hint

The contrapositive is: if $n$ is even, then $n^2$ is even.

## Solution

**Contrapositive.** "If $n^2$ odd, then $n$ odd" is equivalent to "if $n$ even, then $n^2$ even".

**Direct proof of contrapositive.** If $n=2k$, then $n^2=4k^2=2(2k^2)$, which is even.

**Conclusion.** By contraposition, the original statement holds.

@@@ logic-contradiction.md
---
title: Proof by contradiction
category: logic/proof-techniques
level: lycee
difficulty: 2
tags: contradiction, irrationality, sqrt2
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove by contradiction that $\sqrt2$ is irrational.

## Hint

Suppose $\sqrt2=p/q$ with $\gcd(p,q)=1$. Derive that both $p$ and $q$ are even.

## Solution

**Assume.** $\sqrt2=p/q$, $p,q$ coprime positive integers.

**Square.** $2q^2=p^2$, so $p^2$ is even, hence $p$ is even: $p=2k$.

**Substitute.** $2q^2=4k^2$, so $q^2=2k^2$, hence $q$ is even.

**Contradiction.** $p,q$ both even contradicts $\gcd(p,q)=1$.

**Conclusion.** $\sqrt2$ is irrational.

@@@ logic-contrapositive-prime.md
---
title: Contrapositive with primes
category: logic/proof-techniques
level: l1
difficulty: 2
tags: contrapositive, prime, divisibility
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove: if $p$ is prime and $p>2$, then $p$ is odd.

## Hint

The contrapositive: if $p$ is even, then $p$ is not prime or $p\le2$.

## Solution

**Contrapositive.** "If $p$ is prime and $p>2$, then $p$ is odd" is equivalent to "if $p$ is even (and prime), then $p\le2$".

**Proof.** If $p$ is even prime, $p=2k$ for some $k$. Since $p$ is prime and $2\mid p$, either $p=2$ (so $k=1$) or $p$ is composite. Primality forces $p=2$.

**Conclusion.** All primes $p>2$ are odd.

@@@ logic-proof-by-cases.md

title: Proof by cases
category: logic/proof-techniques
level: lycee

tags: proof by cases, parity, absolute value
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove that for all real $x$, $|x|\ge x$.

## Hint

Split into $x\ge0$ and $x<0$.

## Solution

**Case 1: $x\ge0$.** $|x|=x$, so $|x|\ge x$.

**Case 2: $x<0$.** $|x|=-x>0>x$, so $|x|>x$, hence $|x|\ge x$.

**Conclusion.** In all cases $|x|\ge x$.

@@@ logic-proof-cases-parity.md
---
title: A parity case analysis
category: logic/proof-techniques
level: lycee
difficulty: 2
tags: cases, parity, square
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove that the square of any integer has the form $3k$ or $3k+1$, but never $3k+2$.

## Hint

Consider $n\equiv0,1,2\pmod3$.

## Solution

**Cases.**
- $n\equiv0\pmod3$: $n^2\equiv0\pmod3$, so $n^2=3k$.
- $n\equiv1\pmod3$: $n^2\equiv1\pmod3$, so $n^2=3k+1$.
- $n\equiv2\pmod3$: $n^2\equiv4\equiv1\pmod3$, so $n^2=3k+1$.

**Conclusion.** The square of any integer is $\equiv0$ or $1\pmod3$, never $2$.

@@@ logic-equivalence-proof.md
---
title: Proving an equivalence
category: logic/proof-techniques
level: lycee
difficulty: 3
tags: equivalence, iff, proof
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove that for any integer $n$, $n^2$ is even if and only if $n$ is even.

## Hint

Prove both directions: $n$ even $\Rightarrow$ $n^2$ even, and $n^2$ even $\Rightarrow$ $n$ even.

## Solution

**$\Rightarrow$ (n even implies $n^2$ even).** If $n=2k$, then $n^2=4k^2=2(2k^2)$ is even.

**$\Leftarrow$ (n² even implies $n$ even).** Contrapositive: if $n$ is odd, then $n=2k+1$ and $n^2=4k^2+4k+1=2(2k^2+2k)+1$ is odd. So $n^2$ even implies $n$ not odd, i.e. $n$ even.

**Conclusion.** $n^2$ even $\iff$ $n$ even.

@@@ logic-quantifiers-negation.md
---
title: Negating quantifiers
category: logic/proof-techniques
level: lycee
difficulty: 2
tags: quantifiers, negation, logic
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Write the negation of: "$\forall x\in\mathbb{R}$, $\exists y\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $x+y>0$."

## Hint

Swap $\forall\leftrightarrow\exists$ and negate the inner statement.

## Solution

**Negation.**
$$\exists x\in\mathbb{R},\ \forall y\in\mathbb{R},\ x+y\le0.$$

**Interpretation.** There exists some $x$ such that for all $y$, $x+y\le0$. (This is false, since $y$ can be chosen large.)

**Conclusion.** The negation is $\exists x\in\mathbb{R},\forall y\in\mathbb{R},\ x+y\le0$.

@@@ logic-quantifier-order.md
---
title: Order of quantifiers
category: logic/proof-techniques
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: quantifiers, order, logic
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Explain the difference between:
- $P_1$: $\forall x\in\mathbb{R}$, $\exists y\in\mathbb{R}$, $y>x$;
- $P_2$: $\exists y\in\mathbb{R}$, $\forall x\in\mathbb{R}$, $y>x$.

## Hint

$P_1$ allows $y$ to depend on $x$; $P_2$ requires one $y$ for all $x$.

## Solution

**$P_1$ is true.** For every real $x$, choose $y=x+1>x$.

**$P_2$ is false.** No single real number is greater than every real.

**Conclusion.** Order of quantifiers matters: $\forall\exists$ is weaker than $\exists\forall$.

@@@ logic-if-then-converse.md
---
title: Converse, inverse, contrapositive
category: logic/proof-techniques
level: lycee
difficulty: 2
tags: implication, converse, contrapositive
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

For the implication $P\Rightarrow Q$, describe its converse, inverse, and contrapositive. Which are logically equivalent to $P\Rightarrow Q$?

## Hint

Contrapositive is equivalent; converse and inverse are not.

## Solution

**Definitions.**
- Converse: $Q\Rightarrow P$.
- Inverse: $\neg P\Rightarrow\neg Q$.
- Contrapositive: $\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P$.

**Equivalence.** $P\Rightarrow Q$ is equivalent to its contrapositive $\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P$. Converse and inverse are equivalent to each other but not to the original.

**Example.** $P\Rightarrow Q$: "if $n$ even then $n^2$ even". Contrapositive: "if $n^2$ odd then $n$ odd". Converse: "if $n^2$ even then $n$ even" (true here, but not always).

**Conclusion.** Contrapositive is logically equivalent to the implication.

@@@ logic-propositional-tautology.md
---
title: A tautology
category: logic/proof-techniques
level: lycee
difficulty: 2
tags: propositional logic, tautology, truth table
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that $(P\Rightarrow Q)\Leftrightarrow(\neg P\lor Q)$ is a tautology.

## Hint

Build the truth table.

## Solution

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}
  \hline
  P & Q & P \Rightarrow Q & \neg P \lor Q & (P \Rightarrow Q) \Leftrightarrow (\neg P \lor Q) \\
  \hline
  \text{T} & \text{T} & \text{T} & \text{T} & \text{T} \\
  \text{T} & \text{F} & \text{F} & \text{F} & \text{T} \\
  \text{F} & \text{T} & \text{T} & \text{T} & \text{T} \\
  \text{F} & \text{F} & \text{T} & \text{T} & \text{T} \\
  \hline
\end{array}
$$

All entries are T.

**Conclusion.** The formula is a tautology; implication is definable via disjunction.

@@@ logic-de-morgan.md
---
title: De Morgan's laws
category: logic/proof-techniques
level: lycee
difficulty: 1
tags: De Morgan, logic, negation
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

State and prove De Morgan's laws in set theory.

## Hint

Show both inclusions.

## Solution

**Laws.**
- $\overline{A\cup B}=\overline A\cap\overline B$
- $\overline{A\cap B}=\overline A\cup\overline B$

**Proof of first.** $x\in\overline{A\cup B}\iff x\notin A\cup B\iff x\notin A$ and $x\notin B\iff x\in\overline A\cap\overline B$.

**Proof of second.** $x\in\overline{A\cap B}\iff$ not ($x\in A$ and $x\in B$) $\iff x\notin A$ or $x\notin B\iff x\in\overline A\cup\overline B$.

**Conclusion.** Both laws hold.

@@@ logic-russell-paradox.md
---
title: Russell's paradox (statement)
category: logic/proof-techniques
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: Russell paradox, sets, self-reference
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

State Russell's paradox and explain its consequence for naive set theory.

## Hint

Consider the "set of all sets not containing themselves".

## Solution

**Paradox.** Let $R=\{S:S\notin S\}$. Then $R\in R\iff R\notin R$, contradiction.

**Consequence.** Naive comprehension (every property defines a set) is inconsistent. Axiomatic set theory (ZFC) restricts comprehension to avoid self-reference.

**Conclusion.** Russell's paradox motivated modern axiomatic set theory.

@@@ logic-proof-of-existence.md
---
title: Existence proofs
category: logic/proof-techniques
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: existence, constructive, non-constructive
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Give a constructive proof that there exist irrational $x,y$ with $x^y$ rational.

## Hint

Consider $x=\sqrt2$, $y=\sqrt2$; if $x^y$ is rational, done. Otherwise try $x=(\sqrt2)^{\sqrt2}$.

## Solution

**Attempt 1.** $(\sqrt2)^{\sqrt2}$: if this is rational, done with $x=\sqrt2$, $y=\sqrt2$.

**Attempt 2.** If not, set $x=(\sqrt2)^{\sqrt2}$, $y=\sqrt2$. Then $x^y=((\sqrt2)^{\sqrt2})^{\sqrt2}=(\sqrt2)^2=2$, rational. And $x$ is irrational (by assumption).

**Conclusion.** In all cases, there exist irrational $x,y$ with $x^y$ rational. This proof is non-constructive in determining which case holds.

@@@ logic-proof-induction-sum.md
---
title: Proof by induction: sum of first $n$ integers
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: lycee
difficulty: 1
tags: induction, sum, integers
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove by induction that $\sum_{k=1}^{n}k=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ for all $n\ge1$.

## Hint

Base case $n=1$; inductive step: add $n+1$ to both sides.

## Solution

**Base case.** $n=1$: $\sum_{k=1}^1k=1=\frac{1\cdot2}{2}$. ✓

**Inductive step.** Assume $\sum_{k=1}^{n}k=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$. Then
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}k=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}+(n+1)=\frac{n(n+1)+2(n+1)}{2}=\frac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2}.$$

**Conclusion.** By induction, the formula holds for all $n\ge1$.

@@@ logic-induction-sum-squares.md
---
title: Sum of squares by induction
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: lycee
difficulty: 2
tags: induction, sum of squares, integers
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove by induction that $\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$ for all $n\ge1$.

## Hint

Base case $n=1$; inductive step: add $(n+1)^2$ and simplify.

## Solution

**Base case.** $n=1$: $1=\frac{1\cdot2\cdot3}{6}=1$. ✓

**Inductive step.** Assume the formula for $n$. Then
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}k^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}+(n+1)^2.$$
Factor $(n+1)$:
$$=\frac{(n+1)[n(2n+1)+6(n+1)]}{6}=\frac{(n+1)(2n^2+n+6n+6)}{6}=\frac{(n+1)(2n^2+7n+6)}{6}.$$
Factor $2n^2+7n+6=(n+2)(2n+3)$:
$$=\frac{(n+1)(n+2)(2n+3)}{6}.$$
This is the formula for $n+1$.

**Conclusion.** By induction, the formula holds.

@@@ logic-induction-bernoulli.md
---
title: Bernoulli's inequality by induction
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: l1
difficulty: 2
tags: induction, Bernoulli, inequality
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove by induction: for all $x\ge-1$ and all $n\ge1$, $(1+x)^n\ge1+nx$.

## Hint

Base case $n=1$; inductive step: multiply by $1+x\ge0$.

## Solution

**Base case.** $n=1$: $(1+x)^1=1+x$. ✓

**Inductive step.** Assume $(1+x)^n\ge1+nx$. Since $x\ge-1$, $1+x\ge0$, so
$$(1+x)^{n+1}\ge(1+nx)(1+x)=1+(n+1)x+nx^2\ge1+(n+1)x.$$

**Conclusion.** The inequality holds.

@@@ logic-induction-divisibility.md

title: Divisibility by induction
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: induction, divisibility, powers
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove by induction that $3^n-1$ is divisible by $2$ for all $n\ge1$.

## Hint

Write $3^{n+1}-1=3(3^n-1)+2$.

## Solution

**Base case.** $n=1$: $3-1=2$ is even. ✓

**Inductive step.** Assume $3^n-1$ is even. Then
$$3^{n+1}-1=3\cdot3^n-1=3(3^n-1)+2.$$

@@@ logic-induction-strong.md
---
title: Strong induction
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: strong induction, prime factorization
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove that every integer $n\ge2$ is a product of primes (existence of prime factorization) using strong induction.

## Hint

Strong induction: assume the property for all $k<n$, prove for $n$.

## Solution

**Base case.** $n=2$ is prime, so trivially a product of primes.

**Inductive step.** Suppose all integers $2\le k<n$ have prime factorization. For $n$:
- If $n$ is prime, done.
- If $n$ is composite, $n=ab$ with $2\le a,b<n$. By strong induction, $a$ and $b$ are products of primes, so $n=ab$ is too.

**Conclusion.** Every integer $\ge2$ is a product of primes.

## Statement

Base case $n=0$; inductive step.

@@@ logic-induction-geometric-sum.md

## Statement

Prove by induction: for $r\neq1$ and $n\ge1$, $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}r^k=\frac{1-r^n}{1-r}$.

## Hint

Base case $n=1$; inductive step: add $r^n$.

## Solution

**Base case.** $n=1$: $r^0=1=\frac{1-r}{1-r}$. ✓

**Inductive step.** Assume the formula. Then
$$\sum_{k=0}^{n}r^k=\frac{1-r^n}{1-r}+r^n=\frac{1-r^n+r^n(1-r)}{1-r}=\frac{1-r^n+r^n-r^{n+1}}{1-r}=\frac{1-r^{n+1}}{1-r}.$$

**Conclusion.** The formula holds for all $n\ge1$.

@@@ logic-induction-n-factorial.md
---
title: $n!$ vs $2^n$
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: induction, factorial, exponential
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove that $n!>2^n$ for all $n\ge4$.

## Hint

Base case $n=4$; inductive step: multiply by $(n+1)>2$.

## Solution

**Base case.** $n=4$: $4!=24>16=2^4$. ✓

**Inductive step.** Assume $n!>2^n$ with $n\ge4$. Then
$$(n+1)!=(n+1)\cdot n!>(n+1)2^n>2\cdot2^n=2^{n+1},$$
since $n+1>2$.

**Conclusion.** $n!>2^n$ for all $n\ge4$.

@@@ logic-induction-hanoi.md

category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: induction, Hanoi, recurrence
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that the minimum number of moves to solve the Towers of Hanoi with $n$ disks is $2^n-1$.

## Hint

Recurrence $T_n=2T_{n-1}+1$.

## Solution

**Recurrence.** To move $n$ disks: move $n-1$ to auxiliary peg ($T_{n-1}$ moves), move the largest to the target (1 move), move $n-1$ onto it ($T_{n-1}$ moves). So $T_n=2T_{n-1}+1$.

**Solve.** $T_n=2^n-1$ by induction.

@@@ logic-induction-sum-cubes.md

## Statement

Prove by induction: $\sum_{k=1}^n k^3=\left(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^2$.

## Hint

Note that $1^3+\cdots+n^3=(1+\cdots+n)^2$.

## Solution

**Base case.** $n=1$: $1=1^2$. ✓

**Inductive step.** Assume the identity. Then
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}k^3=\frac{n^2(n+1)^2}{4}+(n+1)^3=\frac{(n+1)^2[n^2+4(n+1)]}{4}=\frac{(n+1)^2(n+2)^2}{4}.$$

@@@ logic-induction-product.md

title: Product by induction
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: induction, product, telescoping
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove by induction: $\prod_{k=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{1}{k}\right)=n+1$.

## Hint

$1+1/k=(k+1)/k$, telescoping.

## Solution

**Base case.** $n=1$: $1+1=2$. ✓

**Inductive step.** Assume the product equals $n+1$. Then
$$\prod_{k=1}^{n+1}\left(1+\frac1k\right)=(n+1)\cdot\left(1+\frac{1}{n+1}\right)=(n+1)\cdot\frac{n+2}{n+1}=n+2.$$

**Conclusion.** The product equals $n+1$ for all $n\ge1$.

@@@ logic-induction-inequality.md
---
title: Exponential inequality by induction
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: induction, inequality, exponential
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove that $2^n\ge n^2$ for all $n\ge4$.

## Hint

Base case $n=4$; inductive step: prove $(n+1)^2\le2n^2$ for $n\ge4$ and combine with the inductive hypothesis.

## Solution

**Base case.** $n=4$: $16=2^4\ge4^2=16$. ✓

**Inductive step.** Assume $2^n\ge n^2$. Then $2^{n+1}=2\cdot2^n\ge2n^2$. It suffices to show $2n^2\ge(n+1)^2=n^2+2n+1$, i.e. $n^2-2n-1\ge0$, i.e. $(n-1)^2\ge2$. True for $n\ge3$.

**Conclusion.** $2^n\ge n^2$ for all $n\ge4$.

@@@ logic-induction-strong-fibonacci.md
---
title: Every positive integer is a sum of non-consecutive Fibonacci numbers
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: olympiad
difficulty: 4
tags: induction, Fibonacci, Zeckendorf
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove Zeckendorf's theorem: every positive integer can be expressed uniquely as a sum of non-consecutive Fibonacci numbers (with $F_2=1,F_3=2,\ldots$).

## Hint

Use strong induction: for $n$, pick the largest $F_k\le n$ and apply induction to $n-F_k$.

## Solution

**Existence.** Strong induction on $n$. Choose $F_k$ the largest Fibonacci number $\le n$. Then $n-F_k<F_{k-1}$ (otherwise $F_k+F_{k-1}=F_{k+1}\le n$, contradicting maximality of $F_k$). By induction, $n-F_k$ is a sum of non-consecutive Fibonacci numbers with all indices $<k-1$. Adding $F_k$ gives a valid representation.

**Uniqueness.** Suppose two representations differ; use the recurrence $F_k>F_{k-1}+\cdots+F_1$ for appropriate cases to derive a contradiction.

**Conclusion.** Zeckendorf representations exist and are unique.

@@@ logic-induction-complete-binary-tree.md
---
title: Full binary tree node count
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: induction, binary tree, structural
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove by structural induction: a full binary tree with $n$ internal nodes has $n+1$ leaves.

## Hint

Base case: single node. Inductive step: a tree is a root with two subtrees.

## Solution

**Structural induction.** Base case: a single-node tree has $0$ internal nodes and $1$ leaf. $0+1=1$. ✓

**Inductive step.** Suppose the tree has root with left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$. Let $n_L,n_R$ be internal node counts and $\ell_L,\ell_R$ leaf counts. By induction, $\ell_L=n_L+1$, $\ell_R=n_R+1$. Total internal nodes: $n=n_L+n_R+1$ (including root). Total leaves: $\ell=\ell_L+\ell_R=n_L+1+n_R+1=n+1$.

**Conclusion.** A full binary tree with $n$ internal nodes has $n+1$ leaves.

@@@ logic-induction-strong-division.md
---
title: Existence of quotient and remainder
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: strong induction, division, quotient
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove by strong induction that for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $d\ge1$, there exist unique $q,r$ with $n=qd+r$, $0\le r<d$.

## Hint

Induct on $n$; base case $n<d$.

## Solution

**Base case.** If $n<d$: $q=0$, $r=n$, unique.

**Inductive step.** Suppose all $k<n$ have a unique decomposition. For $n$:
- If $n<d$, done.
- If $n\ge d$: $n-d<n$, so by induction $n-d=qd+r$ with $0\le r<d$. Then $n=(q+1)d+r$, giving existence.

**Uniqueness.** Suppose $n=qd+r=q'd+r'$. Then $(q-q')d=r'-r$ with $|r'-r|<d$; this forces $r=r'$ and $q=q'$.

**Conclusion.** Euclidean division exists and is unique.

@@@ logic-induction-period.md
---
title: Induction and periodicity
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: induction, periodicity, recurrence
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Let $(u_n)$ satisfy $u_{n+2}=u_{n+1}+u_n$ mod $10$, with $u_0=0,u_1=1$. Show the sequence is periodic.

## Hint

The pair $(u_n,u_{n+1})$ takes values in $\{0,\ldots,9\}^2$, finite.

## Solution

**Finiteness.** The state $(u_n,u_{n+1})$ is in $\{0,\ldots,9\}^2$, which has $100$ elements. By pigeonhole, two states repeat.

**Determinism.** The recurrence determines all future states from $(u_n,u_{n+1})$, so once two states coincide, the sequence is periodic from there.

**Conclusion.** The sequence $(u_n\bmod10)$ is periodic.

@@@ logic-induction-tiling.md
---
title: Tiling by induction
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: olympiad
difficulty: 4
tags: induction, tiling, L-tromino
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that any $2^n\times2^n$ board with one square removed can be tiled by L-trominoes (3-square L-shapes).

## Hint

Divide the board into four $2^{n-1}\times2^{n-1}$ quadrants; place one L-tromino at the center to create "removed" squares in each quadrant.

## Solution

**Base case.** $n=1$: $2\times2$ board with one square removed is itself an L-tromino.

**Inductive step.** Divide the $2^n\times2^n$ board into four $2^{n-1}\times2^{n-1}$ quadrants. One contains the removed square. Place one L-tromino covering one corner square of each of the other three quadrants (at the center of the board). Now each quadrant is a $2^{n-1}\times2^{n-1}$ board with one square removed, tiled by induction.

**Conclusion.** The board can be tiled.

@@@ logic-induction-strong-representation.md
---
title: Representation of integers
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: olympiad
difficulty: 4
tags: strong induction, representation, powers
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that every positive integer can be written as a sum of distinct powers of $2$ (binary expansion).

## Hint

Strong induction: if $n$ is even, divide by $2$; if odd, subtract $1$.

## Solution

**Strong induction.** Base case $n=1$: $1=2^0$. ✓

**Inductive step.** Suppose every integer $<n$ has a binary expansion.
- If $n$ is even: $n=2m$ with $m<n$, so $m=\sum 2^{a_i}$; then $n=\sum 2^{a_i+1}$, distinct powers.
- If $n$ is odd: $n-1$ is even and $<n$, so $n-1=\sum 2^{b_i}$; then $n=2^0+\sum 2^{b_i}$, with $0$ distinct from all $b_i$ (since $n-1$ even means all $b_i\ge1$).

**Conclusion.** Every positive integer is a sum of distinct powers of $2$.

@@@ logic-induction-sum-factorials.md
---
title: A factorial identity
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: induction, factorial, identity
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove that $\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\cdot k!=(n+1)!-1$.

## Hint

$k\cdot k!=(k+1)!-k!$, telescoping.

## Solution

**Identity.** $k\cdot k!=(k+1-1)k!=(k+1)!-k!$.

**Sum.** $\sum_{k=1}^n k\cdot k!=\sum_{k=1}^n[(k+1)!-k!]=(n+1)!-1!$.

**Induction alternative.** Base case $n=1$: $1=2!-1=1$. ✓ Inductive step: $\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}k\cdot k!=(n+1)!-1+(n+1)(n+1)!=(n+1)!(n+2)-1=(n+2)!-1$.

**Conclusion.** The identity holds.

@@@ logic-induction-inequality-2.md
---
title: Fibonacci growth bound
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: induction, Fibonacci, growth
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove by induction that $F_n\le\varphi^n$ where $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$ and $F_0=0,F_1=1$.

## Hint

$\varphi^2=\varphi+1$. Strong induction: $F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_n\le\varphi^{n+1}+\varphi^n=\varphi^n(\varphi+1)=\varphi^{n+2}$.

## Solution

**Base cases.** $F_0=0\le1=\varphi^0$. $F_1=1\le\varphi\approx1.618$. ✓

**Inductive step.** Assume $F_n\le\varphi^n$ and $F_{n+1}\le\varphi^{n+1}$. Then
$$F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_n\le\varphi^{n+1}+\varphi^n=\varphi^n(\varphi+1)=\varphi^n\cdot\varphi^2=\varphi^{n+2}.$$

**Conclusion.** $F_n\le\varphi^n$ for all $n$.

@@@ logic-induction-coins.md
---
title: Coins and strong induction
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: induction, coins, Frobenius
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove that every integer $n\ge12$ can be written as $4a+5b$ with $a,b\ge0$.

## Hint

Strong induction, starting with four consecutive integers $12,13,14,15$ as base cases.

## Solution

**Base cases.**
- $12=4\cdot3+5\cdot0$
- $13=4\cdot2+5\cdot1$
- $14=4\cdot1+5\cdot2$
- $15=4\cdot0+5\cdot3$

**Inductive step.** If $n\ge16$ is representable, then $n+4$ is too (add another $4$). Starting from the four base cases, this covers all integers $\ge12$.

**Conclusion.** Every integer $\ge12$ is representable.

@@@ logic-induction-graph.md
---
title: Euler characteristic by induction
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: induction, Euler characteristic, trees
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove that a connected planar graph satisfies $V-E+F=2$ by induction on the number of faces.

## Hint

Remove an edge on a cycle and reduce $F$ by $1$.

## Solution

**Setup.** Induct on the number of edges $E$.

**Base case.** A tree has $F=1$ (only outer face), $V-E+1=1$ (since $E=V-1$), so $V-E+F=V-(V-1)+1=2$. ✓

**Inductive step.** If the graph has a cycle, remove an edge from the cycle: the graph stays connected, $E$ decreases by $1$, and $F$ decreases by $1$ (two faces merge). Both sides of $V-E+F=2$ change by $-1+1=0$, preserving the identity.

**Conclusion.** $V-E+F=2$ for connected planar graphs.

@@@ logic-induction-matrix.md
---
title: Determinant of a matrix by induction
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: induction, matrix, determinant
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove that the determinant of an upper triangular matrix equals the product of its diagonal entries.

## Hint

Expand along the first column; the top entry is the only nonzero.

## Solution

**Base case.** $1\times1$: trivial.

**Inductive step.** For an $n\times n$ upper triangular $T$ with diagonal $t_{11},\ldots,t_{nn}$, expand along the first column: only $t_{11}$ is nonzero (all entries below the diagonal are $0$). Cofactor is $(-1)^{1+1}=1$ times the $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ upper triangular submatrix with diagonal $t_{22},\ldots,t_{nn}$. By induction, this submatrix's determinant is $t_{22}\cdots t_{nn}$.

**Conclusion.** $\det T=t_{11}t_{22}\cdots t_{nn}$.

@@@ logic-induction-real-ind.md
---
title: Real induction (statement)
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: m1
difficulty: 5
tags: real induction, intervals, completeness
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

State the principle of real induction and give an application.

## Hint

If a property holds at $a$, propagates locally, and extends up to limits, then it holds on $[a,b]$.

## Solution

**Principle (real induction).** Let $S\subseteq[a,b]$ satisfy:
1. $a\in S$;
2. If $x\in S$ and $x<b$, then $[x,x+\varepsilon)\subseteq S$ for some $\varepsilon>0$;
3. If $[a,x)\subseteq S$ with $x\le b$, then $x\in S$.
Then $S=[a,b]$.

**Application.** Proving that a continuous function has the intermediate value property.

**Conclusion.** Real induction is a powerful tool for proofs on intervals.

@@@ logic-summary.md
---
title: Summary of logic and proof techniques
category: logic/proof-techniques
level: lycee
difficulty: 2
tags: summary, proof, logic
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Summarize the key proof techniques.

## Hint

Review the main methods.

## Solution

**Direct proof.** Assume hypothesis, derive conclusion step by step.

**Contraposition.** Prove $\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P$ instead of $P\Rightarrow Q$.

**Contradiction.** Assume the negation of the claim, derive a contradiction.

**Cases.** Split into exhaustive cases and prove each.

**Counterexample.** To disprove a universal statement, exhibit one counterexample.

**Induction.** Base case + inductive step (weak, strong, or structural).

**Quantifiers.** $\forall$ and $\exists$; order matters.

**Conclusion.** These techniques cover most standard mathematical proofs.

@@@ logic-summary-induction.md
---
title: Summary of induction
category: logic/proof-techniques/induction
level: lycee
difficulty: 1
tags: summary, induction, techniques
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Summarize the forms of induction.

## Hint

Review weak, strong, structural.

## Solution

**Weak induction.** Base case $P(n_0)$; step $P(n)\Rightarrow P(n+1)$. Concludes $P(n)$ for all $n\ge n_0$.

**Strong induction.** Base case $P(n_0)$; step $[\forall k\in[n_0,n],P(k)]\Rightarrow P(n+1)$. Allows using more hypotheses.

**Structural induction.** For recursively defined objects (trees, formulas, etc.): prove for base objects; step from subobjects to compound objects.

**Well-ordering.** Equivalent to induction: every nonempty subset of $\mathbb{N}$ has a least element.

**Conclusion.** Choose the form best suited to the problem's recursive structure.

## Statement

Let $A(1,2,3)$ and $B(4,6,8)$. Compute the distance $AB$ and the midpoint $M$ of $AB$.

## Hint

$AB=\sqrt{(x_B-x_A)^2+(y_B-y_A)^2+(z_B-z_A)^2}$.

## Solution

**Distance.**
$$AB=\sqrt{(4-1)^2+(6-2)^2+(8-3)^2}=\sqrt{9+16+25}=\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt2.$$

**Midpoint.**
$$M=\left(\frac{1+4}{2},\frac{2+6}{2},\frac{3+8}{2}\right)=\left(\frac52,4,\frac{11}{2}\right).$$

**Conclusion.** $AB=5\sqrt2$, $M=(5/2,4,11/2)$.

## Statement

## Solution

**Cross-sections.** For $z=c$: $x^2+y^2=1+c^2$, circle of radius $\sqrt{1+c^2}$.

**Surface.** A one-sheeted hyperboloid of revolution: it widens as $|z|$ increases, with a "waist" of radius $1$ at $z=0$.

**Conclusion.** The surface is a one-sheeted hyperboloid.

@@@ space-vector-plane-distance.md

title: Distance from a point to a plane using projection
category: geometry/space
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: distance, projection, plane
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Find the orthogonal projection of $P(1,2,3)$ onto the plane $x+y+z=6$.

## Hint

The projection along the normal $\vec n=(1,1,1)$.

## Solution

**Normal.** $\vec n=(1,1,1)$.

**Parametrize perpendicular line.** $P+t\vec n=(1+t,2+t,3+t)$.

**Intersection.** $(1+t)+(2+t)+(3+t)=6$, so $6+3t=6$, $t=0$.

**Projection.** $H=P=(1,2,3)$.

**Conclusion.** $P$ already lies on the plane; the projection is $P$.

@@@ space-plane-line-angle.md

title: Angle between a line and a plane
category: geometry/space
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: angle, line-plane, trigonometry
date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

Compute the angle between the line with direction $\vec d=(1,1,1)$ and the plane with normal $\vec n=(1,0,0)$.

## Hint

$\sin\theta=\dfrac{|\vec d\cdot\vec n|}{\|\vec d\|\|\vec n\|}$.

## Solution

**Compute.** $\vec d\cdot\vec n=1$, $\|\vec d\|=\sqrt3$, $\|\vec n\|=1$.

**Sine.** $\sin\theta=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$.

**Conclusion.** $\theta=\arcsin(1/\sqrt3)\approx35.26^\circ$.

@@@ space-angle-two-lines.md

## Statement

Compute the angle between the lines with directions $\vec d_1=(1,2,-1)$ and $\vec d_2=(2,0,1)$.

## Hint

$\cos\theta=\dfrac{|\vec d_1\cdot\vec d_2|}{\|\vec d_1\|\|\vec d_2\|}$.

## Solution

**Dot product.** $\vec d_1\cdot\vec d_2=2+0-1=1$.

**Norms.** $\|\vec d_1\|=\sqrt{1+4+1}=\sqrt6$, $\|\vec d_2\|=\sqrt{4+0+1}=\sqrt5$.

**Cosine.** $\cos\theta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}$.

**Conclusion.** $\theta=\arccos(1/\sqrt{30})\approx79.5^\circ$.

## Statement

Find the reflection of $P(1,2,3)$ across the plane $x+y+z=0$.

Project onto the plane, then double the projection vector from $P$.

## Solution

**Projection.** Line through $P$ in direction $\vec n=(1,1,1)$: $(1+t, 2+t, 3+t)$. Intersect with plane: $(1+t)+(2+t)+(3+t)=0$, so $t=-2$. $H=(-1,0,1)$.

@@@ space-vector-coplanarity.md

title: Coplanarity of vectors
category: geometry/space
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: coplanarity, triple product, determinant
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that the vectors $\vec u=(1,2,3)$, $\vec v=(2,4,6)$, $\vec w=(1,0,1)$ are coplanar.

## Hint

Coplanar iff the scalar triple product is zero.

## Solution

**Observation.** $\vec v=2\vec u$, so $\vec u$ and $\vec v$ are collinear, hence coplanar with any third vector.

**Triple product.** $\vec u\cdot(\vec v\times\vec w)=0$ since $\vec u,\vec v$ are collinear.

**Conclusion.** The three vectors are coplanar.

@@@ space-parametric-surface.md
---
title: Parametric surfaces
category: geometry/space
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: parametric surface, sphere, torus
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Parametrize the sphere of radius $R$ centered at the origin.

## Hint

Use spherical coordinates with two parameters.

## Solution

**Parametrization.**
$$M(u,v)=(R\sin u\cos v,\ R\sin u\sin v,\ R\cos u),$$
$u\in[0,\pi]$, $v\in[0,2\pi)$.

**Check.** $\|M\|^2=R^2(\sin^2 u\cos^2 v+\sin^2 u\sin^2 v+\cos^2 u)=R^2$.

**Conclusion.** The sphere is parametrized as above.

@@@ space-torus-parametric.md
---
title: Parametrization of a torus
category: geometry/space
level: m1
difficulty: 5
tags: torus, parametric, surface
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Parametrize the torus obtained by revolving a circle of radius $r$ centered at distance $R$ from the axis.

## Hint

Use $(\theta,\phi)$ for the position on the torus and the tube.

## Solution

**Parametrization.**
$$M(\theta,\phi)=((R+r\cos\phi)\cos\theta,\ (R+r\cos\phi)\sin\theta,\ r\sin\phi),$$
$\theta\in[0,2\pi)$, $\phi\in[0,2\pi)$.

**Check.** For each $\phi$, we get a circle of radius $r$ centered at distance $R$ from the $z$-axis, revolved around.

**Conclusion.** The torus has the standard parametrization above.

@@@ space-conic-sections.md
---
title: Conic sections of a cone
category: geometry/space
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: conic, cone, intersection
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Describe how the intersection of a cone with a plane gives each conic type.

## Hint

Depends on the angle of the plane relative to the cone's axis.

## Solution

**Cone.** Double cone $z^2=x^2+y^2$ or $x^2+y^2=r^2z^2$.

**Intersections.**
- Plane perpendicular to axis, not through apex: circle.
- Plane tilted but not parallel to a generatrix: ellipse.
- Plane parallel to exactly one generatrix: parabola.
- Plane parallel to two generatrices (steeper): hyperbola.

**Conclusion.** All three conic types (and the circle) arise from planes cutting a cone.

## Statement

Summarize key facts from 3D geometry.

## Hint

Review the main formulas.

## Solution

**Vectors.**
- Addition, scalar product, dot product, cross product, triple product.
- Norms and angles.

**Lines.**
- Parametric and symmetric equations.
- Distance from point to line: $\|\overrightarrow{AP}\times\vec d\|/\|\vec d\|$.

**Planes.**
- Equation $ax+by+cz=d$; normal $(a,b,c)$.

- Parametrizations.

**Polyhedra.**
- Euler characteristic $V-E+F=2$.
- Five Platonic solids.

@@@ analytic-distance-midpoint.md

## Statement

Let $A(-1,3)$ and $B(5,-1)$. Compute the distance $AB$ and the coordinates of the midpoint $M$.

## Hint

$AB=\sqrt{(x_B-x_A)^2+(y_B-y_A)^2}$ and $M=\left(\frac{x_A+x_B}{2},\frac{y_A+y_B}{2}\right)$.

@@@ analytic-line-two-points.md

## Statement

Find the equation of the line through $A(-2,5)$ and $B(4,-3)$.

## Solution

@@@ analytic-line-parallel-perpendicular.md

## Statement

Let $D:2x-3y+5=0$. Find the line through $A(1,-2)$ parallel to $D$, and the line through $A$ perpendicular to $D$.

## Hint

A line $ax+by+c=0$ has direction vector $(b,-a)$ and normal vector $(a,b)$.

## Solution

**Conclusion.** Parallel: $2x-3y-8=0$; perpendicular: $3x+2y+1=0$.

@@@ analytic-tangent-circle.md
---
title: Tangent to a circle from a point
category: geometry/analytic
level: lycee
difficulty: 3
tags: tangent, circle, distance
date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

Find the tangent line(s) to the circle $x^2+y^2=5$ passing through $P(3,1)$.

## Hint

A line through $P$ has equation $y-1=m(x-3)$; impose tangency (distance from center = radius).

## Solution

**General line.** $mx-y+(1-3m)=0$.

**Tangency condition.** Distance from origin: $\dfrac{|1-3m|}{\sqrt{m^2+1}}=\sqrt5$.

**Square.** $(1-3m)^2=5(m^2+1)$, so $9m^2-6m+1=5m^2+5$, i.e. $4m^2-6m-4=0$, $2m^2-3m-2=0$, $(2m+1)(m-2)=0$.

@@@ analytic-conic-classification.md

title: Classifying a conic

level: l1

tags: conic classification, discriminant, ellipse
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Classify the conic $x^2-4y^2+6x+8y-11=0$.

## Hint

Compute the discriminant of the quadratic form: $B^2-4AC$.

## Solution

**Quadratic form.** $A=1$, $B=0$, $C=-4$; discriminant $B^2-4AC=0+16=16>0$.

**Type.** Positive discriminant: hyperbola.

**Standard form.** Complete the square: $(x+3)^2-9-4((y-1)^2-1)=11$, so $(x+3)^2-4(y-1)^2=16$, i.e. $\frac{(x+3)^2}{16}-\frac{(y-1)^2}{4}=1$.

**Conclusion.** Hyperbola with center $(-3,1)$, transverse axis along $x$, semi-axes $4$ and $2$.

@@@ analytic-conic-rotation.md
---
title: Rotation of axes
category: geometry/analytic
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: rotation, axes, conic
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Find the angle $\theta$ that eliminates the $xy$-term from $5x^2-6xy+5y^2=8$.

## Hint

$\cot 2\theta=(A-C)/B$ with $A=5$, $B=-6$, $C=5$.

## Solution

**Formula.** $\cot 2\theta=(5-5)/(-6)=0$, so $2\theta=\pi/2$, $\theta=\pi/4$.

**Rotate.** With $x=(X-Y)/\sqrt2$, $y=(X+Y)/\sqrt2$:
$$5x^2-6xy+5y^2 = 5\cdot\frac{(X-Y)^2}{2}-6\cdot\frac{(X-Y)(X+Y)}{2}+5\cdot\frac{(X+Y)^2}{2}$$
$=\frac{5}{2}(X^2-2XY+Y^2)-3(X^2-Y^2)+\frac{5}{2}(X^2+2XY+Y^2)$
$=5X^2-6XY+5Y^2-... $ hmm let me recompute. Actually after rotation: $\frac{5}{2}\cdot2(X^2+Y^2)-3(X^2-Y^2)=5(X^2+Y^2)-3X^2+3Y^2=2X^2+8Y^2$.

**Verify.** $\cot 2\theta=0$ correct, eliminating $XY$ term.

**Conclusion.** Rotation by $\theta=\pi/4$ gives $2X^2+8Y^2=8$, i.e. $\frac{X^2}{4}+\frac{Y^2}{1}=1$: an ellipse with semi-axes $2$ and $1$.

Find the center of the conic $x^2+4y^2-2x+8y+1=0$.

## Solution

**Complete.** $(x-1)^2-1+4((y+1)^2-1)+1=0$, so $(x-1)^2+4(y+1)^2=4$, i.e. $\frac{(x-1)^2}{4}+\frac{(y+1)^2}{1}=1$.

**Center.** $(1,-1)$.

**Conclusion.** Center $(1,-1)$; ellipse with semi-axes $2$ and $1$.

@@@ analytic-polar-conic.md
---
title: Polar equation of a conic
category: geometry/analytic
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: polar coordinates, conic, eccentricity
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that the conic with focus at the origin and directrix $x=d$ has polar equation $r=\frac{ed}{1+e\cos\theta}$ where $e$ is the eccentricity.

## Hint

Use $PF=e\cdot PH$ where $H$ is the foot of the perpendicular to the directrix.

## Solution

**Setup.** $F=(0,0)$, directrix $x=d$, $P=(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)$.

**Distance to focus.** $PF=r$.

**Distance to directrix.** $PH=d-r\cos\theta$.

**Conic condition.** $r=e(d-r\cos\theta)$, so $r(1+e\cos\theta)=ed$, i.e. $r=\dfrac{ed}{1+e\cos\theta}$.

**Conclusion.** The polar equation of a conic with focus at origin.

## Statement

@@@ analytic-tangent-ellipse.md
---
title: Tangent to an ellipse
category: geometry/analytic
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: tangent, ellipse, parametric
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Find the tangent to $\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ at the point $(x_0,y_0)$ on the ellipse.

## Hint

Use implicit differentiation or the tangent formula.

## Solution

**Implicit differentiation.** $\frac{2x}{a^2}+\frac{2yy'}{b^2}=0$, so $y'=-\frac{b^2 x_0}{a^2 y_0}$.

**Tangent.** $y-y_0=-\frac{b^2 x_0}{a^2 y_0}(x-x_0)$, i.e. $\frac{xx_0}{a^2}+\frac{yy_0}{b^2}=1$.

**Conclusion.** The tangent at $(x_0,y_0)$ is $\frac{xx_0}{a^2}+\frac{yy_0}{b^2}=1$.

@@@ analytic-shoelace-general.md
---
title: The shoelace formula
category: geometry/analytic
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: shoelace, polygon, area
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

State the shoelace formula for the area of a polygon with vertices $(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)$ in order.

## Hint

Sum cross products of consecutive vertices.

## Solution

**Formula.**
$$\text{Area}=\frac12\left|\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_iy_{i+1}-x_{i+1}y_i)\right|,$$
with $(x_{n+1},y_{n+1})=(x_1,y_1)$.

**Example.** Triangle $(0,0),(4,0),(1,3)$: $\frac12|(0\cdot0-4\cdot0)+(4\cdot3-1\cdot0)+(1\cdot0-0\cdot3)|=\frac12|0+12+0|=6$. ✓

**Conclusion.** The shoelace formula computes polygon area from coordinates.

@@@ analytic-curvature.md

## Statement

Compute the curvature of the parabola $y=x^2$ at the origin.

## Hint

$\kappa=\frac{|y''|}{(1+y'^2)^{3/2}}$.

## Solution

**Derivatives.** $y'=2x$, $y''=2$.

**At origin.** $y'=0$, $y''=2$, so $\kappa=\frac{2}{(1+0)^{3/2}}=2$.

**Radius of curvature.** $R=1/\kappa=1/2$.

@@@ analytic-envelope.md

title: Envelope of a family of lines
category: geometry/analytic
level: m1
difficulty: 5
tags: envelope, family of lines, curve
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Find the envelope of the family of lines $y=tx-t^2/4$ parametrized by $t\in\mathbb{R}$.

## Hint

Differentiate w.r.t. $t$ and solve for $t$ in terms of $x$, then substitute.

## Solution

**Line equation.** $F(x,y,t)=tx-\frac{t^2}{4}-y=0$.

**Envelope condition.** $\partial F/\partial t=x-\frac t2=0$, so $t=2x$.

**Substitute.** $y=2x\cdot x-\frac{(2x)^2}{4}=2x^2-x^2=x^2$.

**Conclusion.** The envelope is the parabola $y=x^2$.

## Statement

Give the parametric equation of the quadratic Bézier curve with control points $P_0=(0,0)$, $P_1=(1,2)$, $P_2=(2,0)$.

## Hint

$B(t)=(1-t)^2P_0+2(1-t)tP_1+t^2P_2$.

## Solution

@@@ analytic-pedal-curve.md

title: The pedal curve

level: m1
difficulty: 5
tags: pedal curve, projections, curve
date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

Compute the pedal curve of a circle $x^2+y^2=r^2$ with respect to its center.

## Hint

The foot of the perpendicular from the center to a tangent line of the circle lies on a concentric circle of radius $r$.

## Solution

**Tangents.** Tangent to the circle at point $P=r(\cos t,\sin t)$: $x\cos t+y\sin t=r$.

**Foot of perpendicular.** The perpendicular from the origin has direction $(\cos t,\sin t)$, so the foot is $r(\cos t,\sin t)$ — which is $P$ itself.

**Pedal curve.** Locus of these feet is the circle $x^2+y^2=r^2$.

**Conclusion.** The pedal curve of a circle with respect to its center is the same circle.

## Statement

Invert the circle $x^2+y^2=2x$ with respect to the unit circle $x^2+y^2=1$.

@@@ analytic-conic-optics.md

title: Optical property of the parabola

level: m1

tags: optical property, parabola, reflection
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that rays parallel to the axis of a parabola $y^2=4px$ reflect to the focus.

## Hint

Use the reflection law and the equality of angles between the incoming ray, tangent, and focal radius.

## Solution

**Tangent.** At point $(x_0,y_0)$ on $y^2=4px$: $y_0y=2p(x+x_0)$, i.e. slope $p/y_0$.

**Angle analysis.** The tangent makes equal angles with the vertical direction (parallel to axis) and the focal radius $(x_0-p, y_0)$.

**Reflection.** By the law of reflection (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection), a ray parallel to the axis reflects along the focal radius, heading to the focus $(p,0)$.

**Conclusion.** The parabola has the optical property: parallel rays focus at the focus.

@@@ analytic-cycloid.md

title: The cycloid
category: geometry/analytic
level: m1
difficulty: 4
tags: cycloid, parametric, rolling
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Parametrize the cycloid generated by a point on a circle of radius $R$ rolling along the $x$-axis.

## Hint

At angle $\theta$, the point's position combines the circle's translation and rotation.

## Solution

**Parametric.**
$$x=R(\theta-\sin\theta), \qquad y=R(1-\cos\theta),$$
$\theta\in\mathbb{R}$.

**Arclength.** $ds=R\sqrt{(1-\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta}\,d\theta=R\sqrt{2-2\cos\theta}\,d\theta=2R\sin(\theta/2)\,d\theta$.

**One arch.** $\theta\in[0,2\pi]$: length $8R$, area under one arch $3\pi R^2$.

**Conclusion.** The cycloid is parametrized by $(R(\theta-\sin\theta), R(1-\cos\theta))$.

## Statement

Give the cubic Bézier curve with control points $P_0=(0,0)$, $P_1=(0,1)$, $P_2=(1,1)$, $P_3=(1,0)$.

## Hint

$B(t)=(1-t)^3P_0+3(1-t)^2tP_1+3(1-t)t^2P_2+t^3P_3$.

## Solution

$$x(t)=3(1-t)t^2+t^3=3t^2-2t^3,$$

@@@ analytic-spline.md
---
title: Spline interpolation (statement)
category: geometry/analytic
level: m1
difficulty: 5
tags: spline, interpolation, smoothness
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Describe cubic spline interpolation and its smoothness.

## Hint

Piecewise cubic polynomials with continuity conditions at knots.

## Solution

**Setup.** Given points $(x_0,y_0),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)$, a cubic spline is a piecewise cubic polynomial $S(x)$ on each $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ such that $S$, $S'$, $S''$ are continuous at internal knots.

**Degrees of freedom.** $4n$ coefficients, $2n$ interpolation + $2(n-1)$ continuity conditions; two more conditions needed (natural spline: $S''(x_0)=S''(x_n)=0$).

**Smoothness.** $C^2$ continuity: the spline is twice continuously differentiable.

**Conclusion.** Cubic splines give smooth, $C^2$ interpolation with minimal curvature.

@@@ analytic-conic-eccentricity.md

date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that the type of conic is determined by its eccentricity $e$.

## Hint

Use focus-directrix definition.

## Solution

**Definition.** $e=c/a$ where $c$ is the focal distance and $a$ the semi-major axis.

**Classification.**
- $e=0$: circle.
- $0<e<1$: ellipse.
- $e=1$: parabola.
- $e>1$: hyperbola.

**Conclusion.** Eccentricity classifies conics.

@@@ analytic-summary.md

title: Summary of analytic geometry
category: geometry/analytic
level: lycee
difficulty: 2
tags: summary, analytic geometry

---

## Statement

Summarize the key formulas and results of analytic geometry.

## Hint

Review the main definitions.

## Solution

**Points and lines.**
- Distance, midpoint.
- Line equations: point-slope, general form $ax+by+c=0$.
- Distance from point to line.

**Circles.**
- Standard and general forms; center, radius.

**Conics.**
- Ellipse: $c^2=a^2-b^2$, foci, eccentricity.
- Hyperbola: $c^2=a^2+b^2$, asymptotes.
- Parabola: focus, directrix.

**Parametric curves.**
- Circle, ellipse, Bézier, cycloid, astroid.

**Change of coordinates.**
- Rotation, translation to simplify conics.

**Conclusion.** Analytic geometry connects algebra and geometry through coordinates.

@@@ plane-triangle-sum-angles.md
---
title: The sum of angles in a triangle
category: geometry/plane
level: lycee
difficulty: 1
tags: triangle, angle sum, Euclidean geometry
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove that the sum of the interior angles of a triangle equals $\pi$ radians ($180^\circ$).

## Hint

Draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side and use alternate interior angles.

## Solution

**Construction.** Let $ABC$ be a triangle. Through $A$, draw the line $L$ parallel to $BC$.

**Alternate angles.** Let $D$ and $E$ be points on $L$ on opposite sides of $A$. Then $\angle DAB=\angle ABC$ (alternate interior, using parallel $L\parallel BC$) and $\angle EAC=\angle ACB$.

**Angle sum.** The angles $\angle DAB$, $\angle BAC$, $\angle EAC$ form a straight angle at $A$ (since $D,A,E$ are collinear). So
$$\angle ABC+\angle BAC+\angle ACB=\angle DAB+\angle BAC+\angle EAC=\pi.$$

**Conclusion.** The sum of the angles of a triangle is $\pi$.

@@@ plane-pythagorean-theorem.md
---
title: The Pythagorean theorem
category: geometry/plane
level: lycee
difficulty: 2
tags: Pythagoras, right triangle, proof
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

In a right triangle with legs $a,b$ and hypotenuse $c$, prove that $a^2+b^2=c^2$.

## Hint

Use the similar-triangle proof: drop the altitude to the hypotenuse and use similarity.

## Solution

**Construction.** Drop the altitude from the right-angle vertex to the hypotenuse, dividing it into segments of length $p$ (adjacent to leg $a$) and $q$ (adjacent to leg $b$), with $p+q=c$.

**Similarity 1.** The triangle formed by $a$, the altitude, and segment $p$ is similar to the original. So $a/c=p/a$, i.e. $a^2=pc$.

**Similarity 2.** Similarly $b^2=qc$.

**Sum.** $a^2+b^2=pc+qc=c(p+q)=c^2$.

**Conclusion.** $a^2+b^2=c^2$.

@@@ plane-thales-theorem.md
---
title: Thales' theorem
category: geometry/plane
level: lycee
difficulty: 2
tags: Thales, right angle, circle
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that if $AB$ is a diameter of a circle and $C$ is any point on the circle distinct from $A,B$, then $\angle ACB=90^\circ$.

## Hint

Let $O$ be the center. The triangles $AOC$ and $BOC$ are isosceles.

## Solution

**Isosceles triangles.** $OA=OC=OB=r$ (radii). So $\triangle AOC$ is isosceles with $\angle OAC=\angle OCA=\alpha$. Similarly $\angle OBC=\angle OCB=\beta$.

**Angle sum.** In $\triangle ABC$: $\alpha+(\alpha+\beta)+\beta=\pi$, so $2\alpha+2\beta=\pi$, i.e. $\alpha+\beta=\pi/2$.

**Conclusion.** $\angle ACB=\alpha+\beta=\pi/2$, so the angle is right.

@@@ plane-law-of-cosines.md
---
title: The law of cosines
category: geometry/plane
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: law of cosines, triangle, proof
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove the law of cosines: in a triangle with sides $a,b,c$ and angle $C$ opposite side $c$,
$$c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C.$$

## Hint

Drop the altitude from $A$ to $BC$ and apply the Pythagorean theorem.

## Solution

**Coordinate setup.** Place $C$ at the origin, $B$ at $(a,0)$, and $A$ at coordinates $(b\cos C, b\sin C)$.

**Distance.** $c^2=|AB|^2=(b\cos C-a)^2+(b\sin C)^2=b^2\cos^2 C-2ab\cos C+a^2+b^2\sin^2 C$.

**Simplify.** $b^2(\cos^2 C+\sin^2 C)=b^2$, so $c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C$.

**Conclusion.** The law of cosines holds.

@@@ plane-law-of-sines.md
---
title: The law of sines
category: geometry/plane
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: law of sines, triangle, circumradius
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove the law of sines: in a triangle with sides $a,b,c$ and opposite angles $A,B,C$,
$$\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{c}{\sin C}=2R,$$
where $R$ is the circumradius.

## Hint

Use the area formula $\text{Area}=\frac12bc\sin A$ and the circumradius relation.

## Solution

**Area.** $S=\frac12bc\sin A=\frac12ca\sin B=\frac12ab\sin C$.

**Divide.** From $\frac12bc\sin A=\frac12ca\sin B$, divide by $\frac12abc$: $\frac{\sin A}{a}=\frac{\sin B}{b}$. Similarly $\frac{\sin B}{b}=\frac{\sin C}{c}$.

**Circumradius.** The relation $a=2R\sin A$ follows from the inscribed angle theorem applied to the diameter through $B$ or via the extended law of sines.

**Conclusion.** $\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{c}{\sin C}=2R$.

@@@ plane-area-triangle-heron.md
---
title: Heron's formula
category: geometry/plane
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: Heron, area, triangle
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove Heron's formula: for a triangle with sides $a,b,c$ and semiperimeter $s=(a+b+c)/2$,
$$\text{Area}=\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}.$$

## Hint

Use the law of cosines to compute $\cos C$, then $\sin C$, and apply $\text{Area}=\frac12ab\sin C$.

## Solution

**Law of cosines.** $\cos C=\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}$.

**Sine.** $\sin^2 C=1-\cos^2 C=\frac{4a^2b^2-(a^2+b^2-c^2)^2}{4a^2b^2}$.

**Factor.** Numerator $=(2ab-(a^2+b^2-c^2))(2ab+(a^2+b^2-c^2))=(c^2-(a-b)^2)((a+b)^2-c^2)$
$=(c-a+b)(c+a-b)(a+b-c)(a+b+c)$.

**Area.** $\text{Area}=\frac12ab\sin C=\frac14\sqrt{(c-a+b)(c+a-b)(a+b-c)(a+b+c)}$.

**Rewrite.** $c-a+b=2(s-a)$, etc., so Area $=\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$.

**Conclusion.** Heron's formula holds.

@@@ plane-similar-triangles.md
---
title: Similar triangles
category: geometry/plane
level: lycee
difficulty: 2
tags: similarity, triangles, ratios
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Two triangles $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ satisfy $\angle A=\angle A'$, $\angle B=\angle B'$, and $\angle C=\angle C'$. Show that the triangles are similar, i.e. $\frac{AB}{A'B'}=\frac{BC}{B'C'}=\frac{AC}{A'C'}$.

## Hint

Place the triangles with corresponding angles aligned; use the parallel-line theorem.

## Solution

**Setup.** Superpose $\triangle ABC$ on $\triangle A'B'C'$ by aligning $A$ with $A'$ and $AB$ along $A'B'$. Since $\angle A=\angle A'$, $AC$ lies along $A'C'$.

**Parallel line.** Since $\angle B=\angle B'$, the line $BC$ is parallel to $B'C'$ (alternate interior angles).

**Thales.** By the parallel-line (Thales) theorem, $\frac{AB}{A'B'}=\frac{AC}{A'C'}=\frac{BC}{B'C'}$.

**Conclusion.** The triangles are similar.

@@@ plane-circles-tangent.md
---
title: Tangent lines to a circle
category: geometry/plane
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: tangent, circle, perpendicular
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that a line is tangent to a circle iff it is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.

## Hint

The shortest distance from the center to any line is measured along the perpendicular.

## Solution

**Forward.** Let $T$ be the point of contact, $O$ the center. If the line is tangent (touches only at $T$), then the distance $OT$ equals $r$. If the line were not perpendicular to $OT$, the perpendicular distance would be $<OT=r$, meaning the line would intersect the circle at two points, contradiction.

**Converse.** Suppose the line at $T$ is perpendicular to $OT$. Any other point $P$ on the line satisfies $OP^2=OT^2+TP^2>r^2$, so $P$ is outside the circle. Thus only $T$ is on the circle.

**Conclusion.** Tangent $\iff$ perpendicular to radius at point of contact.

@@@ plane-inscribed-angle.md
---
title: The inscribed angle theorem
category: geometry/plane
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: inscribed angle, central angle, circle
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that an inscribed angle equals half the central angle subtending the same arc.

## Hint

Join the center to the vertex of the inscribed angle, splitting it into two isosceles triangles.

## Solution

**Setup.** Let $A,B$ be points on a circle with center $O$, and $C$ a point on the circle. Let $\angle ACB$ be the inscribed angle and $\angle AOB$ the central angle (same arc $AB$).

**Case 1 (center inside).** Draw $OC$; the angle $ACB$ splits into $\angle ACO+\angle OCB$. Both $\triangle ACO$ and $\triangle BCO$ are isosceles ($OA=OC=OB$), so $\angle ACO=\angle OAC$ and $\angle OCB=\angle OBC$.

**Sum.** $\angle ACB=\angle ACO+\angle OCB$. And $\angle AOB=2\angle ACB$ (computing via the triangles).

**Conclusion.** The inscribed angle is half the central angle.

**Corollary.** Angles inscribed in the same arc are equal, and an inscribed angle subtending a diameter is $90^\circ$ (Thales).

@@@ plane-power-of-point.md
---
title: Power of a point
category: geometry/plane
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: power of a point, circle, chord
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Let $P$ be a point and $\Gamma$ a circle. A line through $P$ meets $\Gamma$ at $A$ and $B$. Show that $PA\cdot PB$ is constant (independent of the line), equal to $|OP^2-r^2|$ where $O$ is the center and $r$ the radius.

## Hint

Use similar triangles: $\triangle PAC\sim\triangle PDB$ where $C,D$ are the other intersection points of a second line.

## Solution

**Two chords.** Let line $\ell_1$ through $P$ meet $\Gamma$ at $A,B$ and line $\ell_2$ meet at $C,D$.

**Similarity.** The angles $\angle PAC$ and $\angle PDB$ are equal (inscribed angles subtending arc $AC$... careful with the direction). Standard: $\triangle PAC\sim\triangle PDB$.

**Ratio.** $PA/PD=PC/PB$, so $PA\cdot PB=PC\cdot PD$.

**Power.** This constant equals $PA\cdot PB$; when the line passes through $O$, one computes $|OP-r|\cdot|OP+r|=|OP^2-r^2|$.

**Conclusion.** The power of $P$ with respect to $\Gamma$ is $PA\cdot PB=|OP^2-r^2|$ (signed), independent of the line.

@@@ plane-euler-line.md
---
title: The Euler line
category: geometry/plane
level: l1
difficulty: 4
tags: Euler line, centroid, orthocenter, circumcenter
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

In any triangle $ABC$, the centroid $G$, orthocenter $H$, and circumcenter $O$ are collinear, with $GH=2\,OG$.

## Hint

Use vectors with $O$ as origin and exploit $a^2+b^2-c^2$ identities; or use homothety centered at $G$ with ratio $-1/2$.

## Solution

**Homothety.** Consider the homothety $h$ centered at $G$ with ratio $-1/2$. It maps the median from $A$ to the midpoint $M_a$ of $BC$ (since $G$ divides $AM_a$ in ratio $2:1$). Similarly for the other medians.

**Image of $O$.** The image $h(O)=O'$ lies on the line $GO$. One shows $O'$ is the orthocenter $H$: the image of the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ (through $O$) is the altitude from $A$ (passing through $H$), and similarly for other sides.

**Conclusion.** $O$, $G$, $H$ are collinear (Euler line), with $GH=2\,OG$.

@@@ plane-nine-point-circle.md
---
title: The nine-point circle
category: geometry/plane
level: olympiad
difficulty: 5
tags: nine-point circle, Euler, midpoints
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

State and outline a proof of the nine-point circle theorem: the midpoints of the sides, the feet of the altitudes, and the midpoints of the segments from the orthocenter to the vertices all lie on a single circle.

## Hint

Use the homothety centered at the orthocenter with ratio $1/2$; it sends the circumcircle to a smaller circle.

## Solution

**Homothety.** Let $h$ be the homothety centered at $H$ (orthocenter) with ratio $1/2$.

**Images.** $h$ sends $A$ to the midpoint of $AH$, $B$ to midpoint of $BH$, $C$ to midpoint of $CH$ — three of the nine points.

**Circumcircle image.** $h$ sends the circumcircle (passing through $A,B,C$) to a circle through these three midpoints. Its radius is $R/2$.

**Other six points.** One shows (via angle chasing) that the midpoints of sides and feet of altitudes also lie on this circle.

**Conclusion.** The nine points are concyclic; the circle has radius $R/2$ and center at the midpoint of $OH$.

@@@ plane-ptolemy.md
---
title: Ptolemy's theorem
category: geometry/plane
level: olympiad
difficulty: 4
tags: Ptolemy, cyclic quadrilateral, diagonal
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Prove Ptolemy's theorem: if $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral, then
$$AC\cdot BD=AB\cdot CD+BC\cdot AD.$$

## Hint

Construct a point $K$ on $AC$ with $\angle ABK=\angle DBC$, then use similar triangles.

## Solution

**Construction.** On diagonal $AC$, choose $K$ such that $\angle ABK=\angle DBC$.

**Similarity 1.** $\triangle ABK\sim\triangle DBC$ (since $\angle ABK=\angle DBC$ and $\angle BAK=\angle BDC$ by cyclicity). So $AB/BD=AK/DC$, i.e. $AB\cdot DC=BD\cdot AK$.

**Similarity 2.** $\triangle KBC\sim\triangle ABD$: similar angle argument. So $BC/BD=KC/AD$, i.e. $BC\cdot AD=BD\cdot KC$.

**Sum.** $AB\cdot CD+BC\cdot AD=BD(AK+KC)=BD\cdot AC$.

**Conclusion.** $AC\cdot BD=AB\cdot CD+BC\cdot AD$.

@@@ plane-concyclic.md
---
title: Cyclic quadrilaterals
category: geometry/plane
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles, circle
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that a quadrilateral is cyclic (inscribed in a circle) iff its opposite angles sum to $\pi$.

## Hint

$(\Rightarrow)$: inscribed angles subtend complementary arcs. $(\Leftarrow)$: consider the circumcircle of three vertices and use the inscribed angle theorem.

## Solution

**$(\Rightarrow)$.** If $ABCD$ is cyclic, the inscribed angles $\angle DAB$ and $\angle DCB$ subtend complementary arcs $BCD$ and $DAB$. Their measures are half these arcs, summing to half the full circle: $\angle DAB+\angle DCB=\pi$.

**$(\Leftarrow)$.** Suppose $\angle DAB+\angle DCB=\pi$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of $A,B,C$, and $D'$ be the second intersection of $CD$ with $\Gamma$. Then $ABCD'$ is cyclic, so $\angle D'AB+\angle D'CB=\pi$. Combined with the hypothesis, $\angle D'CB=\angle DCB$. This forces $D'=D$ (both on ray $CB$ from $C$).

**Conclusion.** Cyclic $\iff$ opposite angles sum to $\pi$.

@@@ plane-bisector-theorem.md
---
title: The angle bisector theorem
category: geometry/plane
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: angle bisector, triangle, ratio
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

In a triangle $ABC$, let $D$ be the foot of the angle bisector from $A$ on side $BC$. Show that $\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{AB}{AC}$.

## Hint

Apply the law of sines to triangles $ABD$ and $ACD$.

## Solution

**Law of sines in $\triangle ABD$.** $\frac{BD}{\sin\angle BAD}=\frac{AB}{\sin\angle ADB}$.

**Law of sines in $\triangle ACD$.** $\frac{DC}{\sin\angle DAC}=\frac{AC}{\sin\angle ADC}$.

**Ratio.** Since $\angle BAD=\angle DAC$ (bisector) and $\angle ADB+\angle ADC=\pi$ (so $\sin\angle ADB=\sin\angle ADC$), divide:
$$\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{\sin\angle BAD\cdot AB/\sin\angle ADB}{\sin\angle DAC\cdot AC/\sin\angle ADC}=\frac{AB}{AC}.$$

**Conclusion.** $\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{AB}{AC}$.

@@@ plane-median-length.md
---
title: Length of a median
category: geometry/plane
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: median, Apollonius, triangle
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that the median from $A$ to the midpoint $M$ of $BC$ satisfies
$$AM^2=\frac{2AB^2+2AC^2-BC^2}{4}.$$

## Hint

Use the law of cosines on $\triangle ABM$ and $\triangle ACM$, with $\angle AMB+\angle AMC=\pi$.

## Solution

**Law of cosines on $ABM$.** $AB^2=AM^2+BM^2-2\cdot AM\cdot BM\cos\angle AMB$.

**Law of cosines on $ACM$.** $AC^2=AM^2+CM^2-2\cdot AM\cdot CM\cos\angle AMC$.

**Combine.** Since $BM=CM=BC/2$ and $\cos\angle AMC=-\cos\angle AMB$, add the two equations:
$$AB^2+AC^2=2AM^2+\frac{BC^2}{4}+\frac{BC^2}{4}.$$
So $2AM^2=AB^2+AC^2-\frac{BC^2}{2}$, i.e. $AM^2=\frac{2AB^2+2AC^2-BC^2}{4}$.

**Conclusion.** The median formula holds.

@@@ plane-apollonius-circle.md
---
title: The circle of Apollonius
category: geometry/plane
level: olympiad
difficulty: 4
tags: Apollonius, circle, locus
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Let $A,B$ be distinct points and $k>0$, $k\neq1$. Show that the locus of points $M$ with $MA/MB=k$ is a circle.

## Hint

Use coordinates with $A=(0,0)$, $B=(d,0)$. Square the condition $MA^2=k^2 MB^2$ and simplify.

## Solution

**Coordinates.** $A=(0,0)$, $B=(d,0)$, $M=(x,y)$. Condition: $x^2+y^2=k^2((x-d)^2+y^2)$.

**Simplify.** $x^2+y^2=k^2(x^2-2dx+d^2+y^2)$, so $(k^2-1)(x^2+y^2)-2k^2dx+k^2d^2=0$.

**Complete the square.** Divide by $(k^2-1)$:
$$x^2+y^2-\frac{2k^2d}{k^2-1}x=-\frac{k^2d^2}{k^2-1},$$
i.e.
$$\left(x-\frac{k^2d}{k^2-1}\right)^2+y^2=\frac{k^2d^2}{(k^2-1)^2}.$$

**Conclusion.** The locus is a circle with center $\left(\frac{k^2d}{k^2-1},0\right)$ and radius $\frac{kd}{|k^2-1|}$.

@@@ plane-symmedian.md

title: The symmedian (statement)
category: geometry/plane
level: olympiad
difficulty: 4
tags: symmedian, reflection, isogonal
date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

Define the symmedian from $A$ in a triangle and state its key property.

## Hint

Reflection of the median about the angle bisector; the symmedian point $K$ satisfies $KA^2\cdot[\text{small triangle}]=\cdots$.

## Solution

**Definition.** The symmedian from $A$ is the reflection of the median $AM$ across the internal angle bisector at $A$. The three symmedians are concurrent at the Lemoine point $K$.

**Ratio property.** The symmedian meets $BC$ at a point $D$ with $BD/DC=(AB/AC)^2$.

**Conclusion.** Symmedians are isogonal conjugates of medians and arise in optimization problems (minimizing $\sum MA^2$).

@@@ plane-orthocenter.md
---
title: The orthocenter
category: geometry/plane
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: orthocenter, altitudes, triangle
date: 2026-11-03
---

## Statement

Show that the three altitudes of a triangle are concurrent (at the orthocenter).

## Hint

Use Thales' theorem: the quadrilateral formed by two altitude feet and the opposite vertices is cyclic.

## Solution

**Setup.** Let $ABC$ be a triangle, with altitudes $BB'$ (foot on $AC$) and $CC'$ (foot on $AB$). Let $H=BB'\cap CC'$.

**Concyclic.** $\angle BB'C=90^\circ$ and $\angle BC'C=90^\circ$, so $B,C,B',C'$ are concyclic (on the circle with diameter $BC$).

**Angle chase.** $\angle B'HC'=\angle B'BC'$ (subtending arc $B'C'$ in this circle). And $\angle B'HC'=\angle BHC$ (vertical angles). Also $\angle B'BC'=\angle ABC$ (same as $\angle B$).

**Conclusion.** The altitude from $A$ meets $H$: $\angle AHC'=\angle AHC=\angle ABC$, forcing $AH\perp BC$. So $H$ is the orthocenter.

@@@ plane-incenter.md

title: The incenter
category: geometry/plane
level: l1
difficulty: 3
tags: incenter, angle bisectors, incircle
date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

Show that the three angle bisectors of a triangle are concurrent at a point equidistant from the three sides (the incenter).

## Hint

The locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines is the union of the angle bisectors. Apply to two pairs of sides.

## Solution

**Bisector locus.** The angle bisectors of $\angle A$ are the locus of points equidistant from $AB$ and $AC$. Similarly, the angle bisectors of $\angle B$ are the locus equidistant from $BA$ and $BC$.

**Intersection.** Let $I$ be the intersection of the internal bisectors at $A$ and $B$. Then $I$ is equidistant from $AB$, $AC$, and $BC$. So $I$ is equidistant from all three sides, hence lies on the bisector at $C$.

**Conclusion.** The three internal bisectors concur at the incenter $I$, equidistant from all three sides.

date: 2026-11-03

## Statement

Show that the three medians of a triangle are concurrent, and the intersection point divides each median in the ratio $2:1$ from the vertex.

## Hint

Use vectors with centroid at the average; or use the midpoint theorem.

## Solution

**Vector argument.** Let $G=\frac{A+B+C}{3}$ (centroid). The midpoint of $BC$ is $M_a=\frac{B+C}{2}$. Then $G=\frac{A+2M_a}{3}$, so $G$ is on $AM_a$ and $AG:GM_a=2:1$.
